texte.Der richtige Gruß zur richtigen Zeit: The right greeting at the right time
texte.*Buenos días* sagst du am Morgen. *Buena: You say *Buenos días* in the morning. *Buenas noches* works in the evening for both greeting and saying goodbye.
texte.Ausrufe stehen im Spanischen zwischen zw: Exclamations in Spanish are framed by two symbols: *¡Hola!* – the inverted *¡* comes at the start.
texte.Ich, du, er? Einfach weglassen!: I, you, he? Just skip it!
texte.Im Spanischen lässt man *yo* (ich) meist: In Spanish, you often leave out *yo* (I): *Soy de Alemania* literally means "Am from Germany" – the verb form shows who you mean.
texte.*¿Y tú?* („Und du?“) und *Mucho gusto* m: *¿Y tú?* (“And you?”) and *Mucho gusto* make every introduction smooth and friendly.
texte.Vor männlichen Wörtern wird *uno* zu *un: Before masculine words, *uno* becomes *un*: *un café*, but *una cerveza*.
texte.Zahl + Wort + *por favor*: *Dos cervezas: Number + word + *por favor*: *Dos cervezas, por favor* – and you'll sound like a local right away!
texte.*Perdón* benutzt du zum Ansprechen und f: Use *perdón* to get someone's attention or for minor mistakes. *Lo siento* is for genuine apologies (like "I'm sorry").
texte.Auf *gracias* antwortet man fast immer m: You almost always reply to *gracias* with *de nada* – remember them as a pair.
texte.Spanische Wörter sind männlich oder weib: Spanish words are either masculine or feminine: *el café* (the coffee), but *la cerveza* (the beer). It's best to learn the article with the noun!
texte.*La cuenta, por favor* – und schon kommt: *La cuenta, por favor* – and the bill will arrive. Works in any Spanish-speaking restaurant.
texte.*¿Dónde está…?* öffnet dir jede Tür – ob: *¿Dónde está…?* opens every door – whether it's the bathroom, beach, or museum. *Está* means "is" for locations.
texte.Richtungen sagt man mit a la: *a la izqu: Use a la for directions: *a la izquierda* (to the left), *a la derecha* (to the right).
texte.Herkunft geht immer mit *ser*: *Soy de A: Origin always uses *ser*: *Soy de Alemania* (I am from Germany). To say where you currently live, use *vivir en*: *Vivo en Madrid*.
texte.Nationalitäten richten sich nach der Per: Nationalities match the person: a man is *alemán*, a woman *alemana*. And unlike in English, they are written in lowercase.
texte.*Hablo un poco de español* – ein bissche: *Hablo un poco de español* – speaking a little Spanish and admitting it makes any conversation friendlier. Almost always, you'll hear back: *¡Muy bien!*
texte.Spanisch liest man, wie man es schreibt: Spanish is read as it is written
texte.Die beste Nachricht zuerst: Im Spanische: The best news first: In Spanish, almost every letter sounds the same every time. Once you know the rules, you can read ANY word correctly.
texte.Das *h* wird nie gesprochen: *hola* klin: The *h* is never pronounced: *hola* sounds like "ola". The *j*, however, sounds like the English "h" in "hello": *Juan* = "Huan".
texte.*ll* spricht man wie ein deutsches „j\":: *ll* is pronounced like the English "y": *Me llamo* sounds like "Me yamo". And the *ñ* is like "ny" as in "canyon": *España* = "Espanya".
texte.Schwarzer Kaffee heißt *café solo* – „Ka: Black coffee is called *café solo* – "coffee alone." A *cortado* is an espresso with a splash of milk, a Spanish favorite after meals.
texte.*Tostada con tomate* – Röstbrot mit geri: *Tostada con tomate* – toasted bread with grated tomato and olive oil – is THE breakfast in southern Spain. Rarely costs more than €2.50.
texte.In Spanien wird kein Prozentsatz erwarte: In Spain, no percentage is expected. Leaving some change or rounding up is fine – no one will give you a strange look if you don't tip at all.
texte.In fast jeder spanischen Stadt gibt es e: Almost every Spanish city has a market hall. You order loudly over the counter – go for it, that's what this lesson is for.
texte.Mengenangaben brauchen *de*: *un kilo DE: Quantities need *de*: *un kilo DE tomates*, *un litro DE leche*. Leaving out this small word is THE beginner's mistake – not yours anymore.
texte.Weißt du ein Wort nicht? *¿Me pone esto?: Don't know a word? *¿Me pone esto?* ("Can you give me this?") plus pointing works at any market in the world.
texte.Spanisch benutzt *hacer* (machen): *hace: Spanish uses *hacer* (to make/do): *hace sol*, *hace frío* – literally "it makes sun." Only rain has its own verb: *llueve*.
texte.Für „am Montag\" reicht der Artikel: *el: For "on Monday," just use the article: *el lunes*. And *los lunes* means "on Mondays, every Monday." By the way, days of the week are not capitalized.
texte.Wie bei uns: *¡Qué calor!* („Was für ein: Just like for us: *¡Qué calor!* ("What heat!") is Spain's simplest conversation starter – in the elevator, at the bus stop, everywhere.
texte.Ein *rr* ist ein gerolltes R: *perro* (H: A *rr* is a rolled R: *perro* (dog). A single *r* between vowels is just a quick tap: *pero* (but). The difference changes the meaning! If you can't roll it: keep your tongue tip loose behind your upper front teeth and blow.
texte.j und g klingen wie „ch“ in Bach: j and g sound like "ch" in loch
texte.Das *j* ist immer ein Rachenlaut: *traba: The *j* is always a throat sound: *trabajo* sounds like "trabacho." Before *e* and *i*, the *g* also sounds this way: *gente* becomes "chente," but *guitarra* is spelled with a *u* – *guitarra* – to keep it hard.
texte.b und v klingen gleich: b and v sound the same
texte.Für spanische Ohren gibt es keinen Unter: To Spanish ears, there's no difference between *b* and *v*: *vino* and *bino* sound identical. That's why Spaniards often ask when spelling, "¿be o uve?" – is it a B or a V?
texte.Endet ein Wort auf *Vokal*, *n* oder *s*: If a word ends in a *vowel*, *n*, or *s*, the stress is on the second-to-last syllable: *casa*, *examen*, *gracias*. If it ends in any other consonant, it's on the last: *hablar*, *feliz*, *ciudad*.
texte.Ein geschriebener Akzent steht nur dort,: A written accent is only used where the stress deviates from the norm: *café* ends in a vowel but is stressed on the last syllable – hence the accent. *fácil* ends in a consonant but is stressed on the first syllable – hence the accent.
texte.Bei kurzen Wörtern trennt der Akzent die: For short words, the accent separates meanings: *tú* (you) and *tu* (your), *él* (he) and *el* (the), *sí* (yes) and *si* (if). They sound the same when spoken – but are different words in writing.
texte.Die Verbendung verrät schon, wer gemeint: The verb ending already tells you who is meant: *hablo* can only mean “I speak.” So you just say *Hablo español* – not *Yo hablo español*. You only use the pronoun for emphasis: *Yo soy de Alemania, ¿y tú?*
texte.usted ist höflich – und dritte Person: usted is polite – and third person
texte.*usted* heißt „Sie“, wird aber wie *él/e: *usted* means “you” (formal), but it’s conjugated like *él/ella*: *usted habla*, not *usted hablas*. This is confusing at first, but there's a reason: It comes from *vuestra merced* – “Your Grace.”
texte.In Spanien sagt man zu einer Gruppe von: In Spain, you say *vosotros* to a group of friends. Throughout Latin America, you use *ustedes* for both formal and informal situations. Understand both, use one actively.
texte.ser beantwortet: Wer oder was ist das?: ser answers: Who or what is it?
texte.*ser* steht für alles, was jemanden ausm: *ser* is used for everything that defines someone: name, origin, profession, character, appearance, material, time. *Soy Tom. Soy alemán. Soy estudiante. Es la una.* Learn it not as “permanent” – but as the answer to “who or what?”
texte.Nach *ser* steht der Beruf nackt: *Soy p: After *ser*, professions stand alone: *Soy profesor*, *Ella es médica*. You only add *un/una* if there's an adjective: *Es una médica excelente*.
texte.Nach *ser* richtet sich das Adjektiv nac: After *ser*, adjectives match the person: *Tom es alto*, *Ana es alta*, *ellos son altos*. Adjectives ending in *-o* change to *-a*; those ending in *-e* or a consonant stay the same: *joven*, *jóvenes*.
texte.Lerne nie *mesa*, sondern immer *la mesa: Never learn *mesa* alone, always learn *la mesa*. You can't guess the gender – *la mesa* is feminine, even though "table" in English is neutral. Learn the article with the noun, and you'll never have to guess.
texte.Die Faustregel und ihre Grenzen: The rule of thumb and its limits
texte.Endet ein Wort auf *-o*, ist es meist mä: If a word ends in *-o*, it's usually masculine (*el libro*); if it ends in *-a*, it's usually feminine (*la mesa*). Also, *-ción*, *-dad*, and *-tad* are always feminine: *la ciudad*. Words ending in *-e* or a consonant need to be learned individually.
texte.*el problema*, *el idioma*, *el día*, *e: *el problema*, *el idioma*, *el día*, *el mapa* are masculine despite ending in *-a*. Conversely, *la mano* is feminine despite ending in *-o*. There aren't many, but they're words you use all the time.
texte.Endet ein Wort auf einen Vokal, hängst d: If a word ends in a vowel, add *-s*: *amigo → amigos*, but *flor* ends in a consonant and gets *-es*: *flores*. The article changes too: *el → los*, *la → las*.
texte.Wörter auf *-z* schreiben in der Mehrzah: Words ending in *-z* change to *-ces* in plural: *la voz → las voces*, *el lápiz → los lápices*, *la vez → las veces*. The pronunciation barely changes – it's a spelling rule, not a pronunciation rule.
texte.Durch die neue Silbe verschiebt sich die: When a new syllable is added, the stress shifts – and the accent follows the rule from Lesson 4. *joven* becomes *jóvenes* (accent added), *el inglés* becomes *los ingleses* (accent removed).
texte.Im Spanischen ändert sich die Wortstellu: In Spanish, the word order doesn't change for questions. *Tú hablas español* and *¿Tú hablas español?* look the same. The *¿* at the beginning signals a question is coming – in English, we rely on intonation or auxiliary verbs.
texte.Fragewörter tragen immer einen Akzent: Question words always have an accent
texte.*qué*, *dónde*, *cómo* mit Akzent sind F: *qué*, *dónde*, *cómo* with an accent are question words. Without an accent, they mean something else: *que* (that), *donde* (where ... is), *como* (like, I eat). The accent mark distinguishes function, not pronunciation.
texte.Man kann jeden Satz durch die Stimme zur: You can turn any statement into a question with your voice: *¿Vienes mañana?* Your voice rises at the end. For a “right?” you add *¿verdad?* or *¿no?*: *Hablas español, ¿verdad?*
texte.Streiche die Endung *-ar* und hänge an,: Remove the ending *-ar* and add who is speaking: *habl-o*, *habl-as*, *habl-a*, *habl-amos*, *habl-áis*, *habl-an*. These six endings apply to every regular *-ar* verb – just like *trabajar*, *estudiar*, and *cocinar*.
texte.Die Endung sagt schon, wer gemeint ist:: The ending already tells you who is speaking: *hablo* can only mean “I speak.” That's why you say *Hablo español*, not *Yo hablo español*. The pronoun is only added for emphasis or comparison.
texte.*Hablo español* heißt „ich spreche Spani: *Hablo español* means "I speak Spanish," "I am speaking," and "I am currently speaking." Spanish doesn't need a continuous form for this – the simple present covers it.
texte.Das no steht vor dem Verb: The no comes before the verb
texte.Anders als im Deutschen wandert die Vern: Unlike in English, the negation comes first: *No hablo francés* – literally "not I speak French." Nothing fits between *no* and the verb except a pronoun.
texte.Steht ein Wort wie *nada*, *nadie* oder: If a word like *nada*, *nadie*, or *nunca* follows the verb, you MUST have a *no* before it: *No veo nada.* If the word moves to the front, the *no* disappears: *Nunca veo nada.* Both are correct, just not mixed.
texte.Auf einen positiven Satz antwortet man m: Respond to a positive statement with *también*: "Hablo español." – "Yo también." Respond to a negative one with *tampoco*: "No hablo francés." – "Yo tampoco." Saying *también* here accidentally means the opposite.
texte.estar beantwortet: Wo? Und wie gerade?: estar answers: Where? And how right now?
texte.*estar* steht für den Ort und für den Zu: *estar* is for location and current state: *Estoy en Madrid.* *Estoy cansado.* *La llave está aquí.* If something changes soon or is a snapshot, use *estar*.
texte.ser oder estar – die kurze Faustregel: ser or estar – the quick rule of thumb
texte.*ser* sagt, WER oder WAS etwas ist: *Ana: *ser* tells WHO or WHAT something is: *Ana es profesora.* *estar* tells WHERE it is or HOW it is right now: *Ana está en la escuela.* For location, there's no exception – it's always *estar*.
texte.Mit *ser* wird ein Adjektiv zum Charakte: With *ser*, an adjective describes character, with *estar*, it describes mood: *Es aburrido* means "he is boring," *Está aburrido* means "he is bored." Similarly: *es guapa* (she is pretty) and *está guapa* (she looks pretty today).
texte.Die Frage entscheidet, nicht das Gefühl: The question decides, not the feeling
texte.Frag dich: WER oder WAS ist das? Dann *s: Ask yourself: WHO or WHAT is it? Then use *ser*. WHERE is it or HOW is it doing right now? Then use *estar*. *Ana es profesora* (what she is), *Ana está en clase* (where she is), *Ana está cansada* (how she feels). Forget “permanent vs. temporary” – *estar muerto* is quite permanent.
texte.Bei manchen Adjektiven ändert das Verb d: With some adjectives, the verb changes the meaning: *es aburrido* (he is boring) vs. *está aburrido* (he is bored). *Es listo* (smart) vs. *está listo* (ready). *Es rico* (rich) vs. *está rico* (tastes good). *Es malo* (bad) vs. *está malo* (sick).
texte.Beim Ort gilt sonst immer *estar* – aber: For location, you usually use *estar* – but events are the exception: *La fiesta es en mi casa.* *El concierto es en el parque.* The reason: A party doesn’t just sit somewhere, it takes place. A table, on the other hand: *La mesa está en la cocina.*
texte.*hay* sagt, DASS es etwas gibt – der Zuh: *hay* says THAT something exists – the listener doesn’t know it yet: *Hay una farmacia aquí.* *está* says WHERE something known is: *La farmacia está al lado del banco.* First introduce, then locate.
texte.*hay* verträgt keinen bestimmten Artikel: *hay* doesn’t work with a definite article. Correct is *hay un banco*, *hay dos bancos*, *hay bancos* – incorrect is *hay el banco*. As soon as you say *el* or *la*, you need *está*.
texte.Egal ob eines oder zwanzig: *Hay un coch: Whether one or twenty: *Hay un coche.* *Hay veinte coches.* There’s no “hays”. With *estar*, the number matters: *El coche está…* vs. *Los coches están…*
texte.Der Stamm wechselt – aber nicht überall: The stem changes – but not everywhere
texte.*tener* ist unregelmäßig: *tengo*, *tien: *tener* is irregular: *tengo*, *tienes*, *tiene*, *tenemos*, *tenéis*, *tienen*. The *e* changes to *ie* where the stress falls on it. For *nosotros* and *vosotros*, the stress is elsewhere – so it stays *tenemos* and *tenéis*.
texte.Man hat Jahre, man ist sie nicht: You have years, you don't 'be' them
texte.Das Alter steht mit *tener*, nicht mit *: Age is expressed with *tener*, not *ser*: *Tengo treinta años.* *¿Cuántos años tienes?* Saying *Soy treinta* would be as incorrect as saying "I am thirty years have" in English. And you can't leave out *años*.
texte.Hunger, Durst, Eile – alles mit tener: Hunger, thirst, hurry – all with tener
texte.Wo das Deutsche „sein“ nimmt, nimmt das: Where English uses "to be," Spanish often uses *tener*: *tener hambre* (to be hungry), *tener sed* (to be thirsty), *tener frío* (to be cold), *tener calor* (to be hot), *tener sueño* (to be sleepy), *tener prisa* (to be in a hurry), *tener miedo* (to be afraid).
texte.Bis 29 steht alles zusammen: *veintiuno*: Up to 29, everything is written together: *veintiuno*, *veintidós*. From 30 onwards, you add a *y* and write separately: *treinta y uno*, *cuarenta y cinco*, *noventa y nueve*. There's no *treintaiuno*.
texte.Genau hundert heißt *cien*: *cien euros*: Exactly one hundred is *cien*: *cien euros*, *cien años*. Add something, and it becomes *ciento*: *ciento uno*, *ciento cincuenta*. And there's NO *y* between hundreds and the rest: *ciento veinte*, not *ciento y veinte*.
texte.Ab zweihundert passt sich die Zahl an: *: From two hundred onwards, the number agrees: *doscientos euros*, but *doscientas personas*. Three are irregular and need to be learned: *quinientos* (500), *setecientos* (700), *novecientos* (900).
texte.Eins ist Einzahl, alles andere Mehrzahl: One is singular, everything else is plural
texte.Die Uhrzeit steht mit *ser* – und richte: Time is expressed with *ser* – and it depends on the hour: *Es la una* (one o'clock), but *Son las dos*, *Son las siete*. The *la* and *las* refer to *hora* and *horas*, which is why they are feminine.
texte.Erst nach halb wird abgezogen: After half past, you subtract from the next hour
texte.Bis zur halben Stunde zählt man dazu: *l: Up to half past, you add minutes: *las tres y diez*, *las tres y media*. After that, you subtract from the next hour: *las cuatro menos veinte*, *las cuatro menos cuarto*. For 'at' a specific time, use *a*: *a las ocho*.
texte.Wochentage tragen einen Artikel: Days of the week use an article
texte.Für „am Montag“ sagt man *el lunes*, für: For 'on Monday', you say *el lunes*, for 'on Mondays', *los lunes*. There's no *en lunes*. Days are lowercase, and *sábado* and *domingo* form the plural with *-s*, the others stay the same: *los lunes*.
texte.Tausende Wörter bekommst du geschenkt: Thousands of words are a gift to you
texte.Spanisch und Deutsch teilen sich einen r: Spanish and English share a huge stock of Latin words. *hotel*, *restaurante*, *hospital*, *animal*, *natural* – you don't need to learn these, just pronounce them. If you know English, you'll understand even more.
texte.Deutsch *-tion* wird spanisch *-ción*: *: English *-tion* becomes Spanish *-ción*: *Information → información*, *Nation → nación*. English *-ty* becomes *-dad*: *University → universidad*, *Possibility → posibilidad*. Both groups are **always feminine**: *la información*, *la universidad*.
texte.Jede Lektion bringt neue Wörter, einen D: Each lesson brings new words, a dialogue, and exercises – and revisits three old words, so nothing gets lost. With 80% correct answers, you complete a lesson. Below that, the app suggests another round but doesn't block you.
texte.Die vier Sätze, die dich retten: The four sentences that save you
texte.Wer diese vier kann, bleibt in jedem Ges: If you know these four, you can stay in any conversation: *No entiendo.* *¿Puedes repetir, por favor?* *Más despacio.* *¿Cómo se dice … en español?* They're more important than a hundred vocabulary words – because they keep the conversation going, instead of ending it.
texte.Aus Modul 1 hast du vier Bausteine: *ser: From Module 1, you have four building blocks: *ser* (who I am), *estar* (where I am, how I feel), *tener* (what I have, how old I am), and *hay* (what there is). With these: *Soy Tom, tengo veinticinco años, estoy en Madrid y aquí hay mucha gente.*
texte.*Vale* heißt okay, einverstanden, versta: *Vale* means okay, agreed, understood, good. In Spain, you hear it constantly – in Latin America, you might hear *bueno*, *dale*, or *listo* instead. Just one word can reveal where someone is from.
texte.Streiche *-er* und hänge an: *com-o*, *c: Drop *-er* and add: *com-o*, *com-es*, *com-e*, *com-emos*, *com-éis*, *com-en*. Except for *nosotros* and *vosotros*, the vowels are the same as with *-ar*, just with *e* instead of *a*.
texte.*viv-o*, *viv-es*, *viv-e*, *viv-imos*,: *viv-o*, *viv-es*, *viv-e*, *viv-imos*, *viv-ís*, *viv-en*. Four out of six forms are identical to *-er*! Only *nosotros* and *vosotros* differ: *comemos* versus *vivimos*, *coméis* versus *vivís*.
texte.Was du dir wirklich merken musst: What you really need to remember
texte.Statt drei Tabellen zu lernen, merk dir:: Instead of learning three tables, remember: The *I* form ends in *-o* in all three groups. And *-er* and *-ir* only differ in two out of six forms. That's much less than it seems.
texte.Das Pronomen steht vor dem Verb: The pronoun comes before the verb
texte.Reflexive Verben tragen im Wörterbuch ei: Reflexive verbs have a *-se* in the dictionary: *levantarse*. When conjugating, it moves to the front and adjusts: *me levanto*, *te levantas*, *se levanta*, *nos levantamos*, *os levantáis*, *se levantan*.
texte.Dasselbe Verb, mit und ohne: The same verb, with and without
texte.Das *se* sagt, dass die Handlung auf ein: The *se* indicates that the action reflects back on oneself. *Despierto a mi hijo* – I wake my son. *Me despierto* – I wake up. *Lavo el coche* versus *me lavo* works the same way.
texte.Mit *primero*, *luego*, *después* und *p: With *primero*, *luego*, *después*, and *por fin*, you sequence events: *Primero me levanto, luego desayuno, después salgo de casa y por fin llego al trabajo.* This way, you narrate an entire day.
texte.Erst was es gibt, dann wo es steht: First what it is, then where it is
texte.Beim Beschreiben wechselst du ständig: *: When describing, you constantly switch: *En mi piso hay un balcón* (there is a) and *El balcón está a la izquierda* (where it is). You almost always describe a room in this order – first introduce, then locate.
texte.Zu den Präpositionen aus Lektion 18 komm: To the prepositions from lesson 18, add two vertical ones: *encima de* (on, above) and *debajo de* (under). *El libro está encima de la mesa.* *Los zapatos están debajo de la cama.*
texte.Der *piso* ist die normale Etagenwohnung: The *piso* is the standard apartment in Spain. An *apartamento* is smaller, often a vacation rental. *Casa* actually means house – but *voy a casa* simply means "I'm going home," no matter where you live.
texte.Sie richten sich nach dem Ding, nicht na: They agree with the thing, not with you
texte.*mi*, *tu* und *su* haben nur eine Mehrz: *mi*, *tu*, and *su* only have one plural form: *mi hermano*, *mis hermanos*. They don't ask if YOU are male, but how many things there are. *Nuestro* is the exception and fully adapts: *nuestro piso*, *nuestra casa*, *nuestros hijos*.
texte.*su* heißt sein, ihr, Ihr, ihr (Mehrzahl: *su* means his, her, your (formal), their – depending on context. *Su padre* can be the father of him, her, you, or several people. If it gets unclear, you clarify: *el padre de Ana*.
texte.Ana García López heißt so, weil ihr Vate: Ana García López is named this way because her father's last name is García and her mother's is López. In Spain, names don't change upon marriage. She's addressed by the first: *señora García*.
texte.Im Deutschen sagst du „ein rotes Auto“,: In English, you say "a red car," but in Spanish, it's *un coche rojo*. This reversal is the rule, not the exception: *una casa grande*, *un libro nuevo*, *el pelo largo*.
texte.Adjektive auf *-o* wechseln zu *-a* und: Adjectives ending in *-o* change to *-a* for feminine and form plurals: *rojo, roja, rojos, rojas*. Those ending in *-e* or a consonant don't change for gender, only number: *verde, verdes*, *azul, azules*.
texte.Ein paar Adjektive stehen vorn und bedeu: Some adjectives change meaning based on position: *un amigo viejo* is an old man, *un viejo amigo* is a long-time friend. *Un coche nuevo* is brand new, *un nuevo coche* is just new to you.
texte.llevar heißt tragen – dreifach: llevar means to wear – and more
texte.*llevar* deckt drei deutsche Wörter ab:: *llevar* covers three English verbs: to wear clothes (*llevo una camisa*), to take something with you (*llevo el paraguas*), and to bring someone (*te llevo a casa*). Context decides.
texte.*llevar* beschreibt den Zustand: *Llevo: *llevar* describes the state: *Llevo una chaqueta* – I'm wearing it. *ponerse* is the action: *Me pongo la chaqueta* – I'm putting it on. And *quitarse* is the opposite: *Me quito los zapatos.*
texte.Wie im Deutschen „die Hosen“ stehen eini: Just like in English "pants," some clothing items are plural in Spanish: *los pantalones*, *las gafas* (glasses), *los vaqueros* (jeans). The verb agrees: *Los pantalones son caros*, not *es caro*.
texte.Wo das Deutsche „meine Hände“ sagt, sagt: Where English says "my hands," Spanish uses *las manos*: *Me lavo las manos.* *Me duele la cabeza.* The *me* already indicates whose head it is – saying *mi cabeza* sounds like you have several to choose from.
texte.Nicht du tust weh, sondern der Körpertei: It's not you who hurts, but the body part that hurts YOU: *Me duele la cabeza* (singular), *Me duelen los pies* (plural). The verb agrees with what hurts – not with the person.
texte.Mit *tener* nennst du das, was du hast:: With *tener*, you name what you have: *tengo fiebre*, *tengo tos*, *tengo dolor de cabeza*. With *estar*, you describe the state: *estoy resfriado*, *estoy enfermo*, *estoy cansado*. Both are used, just never mixed.
texte.Spanisch sagt nicht „ich mag den Kaffee“: Spanish doesn't say "I like coffee," but "coffee pleases me": *Me gusta el café.* You're not the subject – the coffee is. Just like with *doler* from the last lesson.
texte.Das Verb richtet sich nach dem, was gefä: The verb agrees with what pleases: *Me gusta el libro* (one), *Me gustan los libros* (several). If a verb follows, it stays *gusta*: *Me gusta bailar*, *Me gusta leer y escribir* – even with two.
texte.Auf *Me gusta el fútbol* antwortest du m: To *Me gusta el fútbol*, you reply with *A mí también* (me too) or *A mí no* (not me). To *No me gusta*, use *A mí tampoco* (me neither) or *A mí sí* (I do). Four short replies to get you through any situation.
texte.Das Deutsche kennt „dieser“ und „jener“,: English uses "this" and "that," but Spanish has three levels: *este* (near me), *ese* (near you), *aquel* (far from both of us). In a store, you can point out what you mean without words.
texte.*este queso*, *esta leche*, *estos huevo: *este queso*, *esta leche*, *estos huevos*, *estas frutas*. The same goes for *ese/esa/esos/esas* and *aquel/aquella/aquellos/aquellas*. Remember: The feminine form of *este* is *esta* – no extra *e* needed.
texte.Was man an der Kasse hört: What you hear at the checkout
texte.*¿Tiene tarjeta de fidelidad?* (Kundenka: *¿Tiene tarjeta de fidelidad?* (loyalty card), *¿Necesita bolsa?*, *¿Efectivo o tarjeta?*, *Son doce con cincuenta.* The last sentence means €12.50 – the comma is spoken as *con*.
texte.Der Befehl ist fast die er-Form: The command is almost the he-form
texte.Für „schneide!“ nimmst du die *él*-Form:: For "cut!" you use the *él* form: *él corta* becomes *¡Corta!* It's the same for *-er* and *-ir* verbs: *él come* becomes *¡Come!*, *él añade* becomes *¡Añade!* Just one letter changes a statement to a command.
texte.Spanische Rezepte stehen fast immer in d: Spanish recipes almost always use the informal "you" form: *Corta, añade, mezcla, fríe.* In cookbooks, you might also find the infinitive – *cortar la cebolla* – which feels more neutral and impersonal.
texte.*Corta las patatas y la cebolla. Fríe to: *Corta las patatas y la cebolla. Fríe todo en aceite. Mezcla con seis huevos. Cuaja en la sartén.* That's all it takes – and you've cooked Spain's most famous dish.
texte.Nach *poder*, *querer*, *tener que* und: After *poder*, *querer*, *tener que*, and *saber*, the second verb stays in its base form: *Quiero comer*, *Puedo ayudar*, *Tengo que salir*. Only the first verb changes – the second stays as it is in the dictionary.
texte.poder und querer wechseln den Stamm: poder and querer change their stem
texte.Beide gehören zu den Verben mit Vokalwec: Both are stem-changing verbs: *puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden* and *quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren*. For *nosotros* and *vosotros*, the stem stays the same – just like with *tener*.
texte.Ein nacktes *No puedo* klingt hart. Übli: A plain *No puedo* sounds blunt. It's common to say: *Es que no puedo, lo siento.* Or offer an alternative: *Hoy no puedo, pero quizás el domingo.* The phrase *es que* is the Spanish way to introduce an explanation.
texte.Wem? Das steht vor dem Verb: To whom? That comes before the verb
texte.*me*, *te*, *le*, *nos*, *os*, *les* sag: *me*, *te*, *le*, *nos*, *os*, *les* indicate TO WHOM something happens: *Me trae la cuenta* (to me), *Nos trae la carta* (to us). They come before the conjugated verb – or attach to an infinitive: *¿Puede traerme la cuenta?*
texte.Beim Menü gliederst du mit *de*: *De pri: Use *de* to structure your order: *De primero, ensalada. De segundo, pollo. De postre, fruta.* It's shorter than full sentences and sounds just like in a local spot. For drinks, say *para beber*.
In Spain, tipping isn't mandatory. A few coins or rounding up is common – 10% is considered generous. In bars, you often leave nothing, but in restaurants, a bit more.
texte.para zeigt nach vorn, por nach hinten: para looks forward, por looks back
texte.*para* nennt Ziel, Zweck oder Empfänger:: *para* indicates purpose, goal, or recipient: *para ti*, *para mañana*, *para aprender*. *por* indicates reason, exchange, or route: *por diez euros*, *por eso*, *gracias por todo*. Tip: *para* = for what, *por* = by what or against what.
texte.Was an der Kasse gesagt wird: What is said at the checkout
texte.*¿Cómo va a pagar?* – *En efectivo* oder: *¿Cómo va a pagar?* – *En efectivo* or *con tarjeta*. Then: *Introduzca la tarjeta*, *Firme aquí*, *Aquí tiene el recibo*. For small amounts, you might hear *Es que no tengo cambio* – the server doesn't have change.
texte.Getrennte Rechnungen sind unüblich. Man: Separate bills are uncommon. You say *pagamos a medias* (split the bill) or *hoy invito yo* (it's my treat today). When treating, one person really pays for everything – and it switches next time.
texte.Drei Bausteine für jeden Vergleich: Three building blocks for every comparison
texte.*más … que* (mehr als), *menos … que* (w: *más … que* (more than), *menos … que* (less than), *tan … como* (as … as). The adjective goes in between: *más barato que*, *menos caro que*, *tan bonito como*. With numbers, *que* becomes *de*: *más de veinte euros*.
texte.Vier Wörter, die aus der Reihe tanzen: Four words that break the pattern
texte.Statt *más bueno* sagt man *mejor*, stat: Instead of *más bueno*, you say *mejor*; instead of *más malo*, you say *peor*. Similarly, *mayor* (older, bigger) and *menor* (younger, smaller). *Mi hermano mayor* is the older brother – not the bigger one.
texte.Was im Laden gefragt wird: What is asked in the store
texte.*¿Qué talla usa?* (Welche Größe?), *¿Se: *¿Qué talla usa?* (What size?), *¿Se lo quiere probar?* (Want to try it on?), *¿Le queda bien?* (Does it fit?). Responses: *Me queda grande / pequeño / bien.* And for exchanges: *¿Tiene el recibo?*
texte.Drei Teile, und du kannst die Zukunft: Three parts, and you can talk about the future
texte.*ir* + *a* + Infinitiv: *Voy a comer.* *: *ir* + *a* + Infinitive: *Voy a comer.* *Vas a trabajar.* *Vamos a salir.* The *a* must never be missing – *voy comer* is incorrect. This is the only future form you need for everyday use.
texte.*voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van* – vom I: *voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van* – nothing remains of the infinitive *ir*. You have to memorize it. On the bright side, it's one of the few verbs where everything is truly different.
texte.ir a heißt auch einfach hingehen: ir a also simply means to go to
texte.Vor einem Ort bedeutet *ir a* schlicht „: Before a place, *ir a* simply means "to go to": *Voy a Madrid*, *Voy al cine* (a + el = al). Before a verb, it turns into the future tense: *Voy a comer*. Same two words, two meanings – the rest of the sentence decides.
texte.quedar heißt sich treffen – ohne Reflexi: quedar means to meet – no reflexive pronoun needed
texte.*¿Quedamos a las ocho?* heißt „treffen w: *¿Quedamos a las ocho?* means "shall we meet at eight?". No *nos* needed. But *quedarse* with *se* means something else: to stay. *Me quedo en casa* – I stay at home.
texte.*¿Te apetece un café?* – wörtlich „reizt: *¿Te apetece un café?* – literally "does a coffee appeal to you?". The sentence is flipped: *me apetece*, *te apetece*, *le apetece*. For plural: *me apetecen las tapas*.
texte.Bei privaten Verabredungen sind zehn bis: For social meetings, being ten to fifteen minutes late is normal and no one apologizes for it. This doesn't apply to appointments with doctors, authorities, or at work – punctuality is expected there.
texte.Im Monat heißt en, am Tag heißt el: In the month is en, on the day is el
texte.Für Monate und Jahreszeiten steht *en*:: For months and seasons, use *en*: *en enero*, *en verano*. For weekdays, use the article: *el lunes*. And dates need *de*: *el quince de mayo*. Three patterns to keep straight.
texte.Anders als im Deutschen zählt man normal: Unlike in English, you count normally in Spanish: *el uno de enero*, *el quince de mayo*, *el treinta y uno de diciembre*. No "first," no period after the number. Only the month name is lowercase.
texte.Im August verlassen die Städte ihre Bewo: In August, cities empty out: shops close for weeks, offices operate with minimal staff. If you need to get something done in August, call ahead – *¿Están abiertos en agosto?*
texte.Bis jetzt hast du kurze Sätze gebaut. *p: So far, you've built short sentences. *porque*, *pero*, *cuando*, *aunque*, and *así que* connect them: *No puedo ir porque tengo que trabajar, pero quizás el domingo sí.* One sentence instead of three – and you sound instantly more fluent.
texte.Getrennt und mit Akzent fragt man: *¿Por: Separated and with an accent, you ask: *¿Por qué no vienes?* Together and without an accent, you answer: *Porque estoy cansado.* A space and a mark separate question from answer.
texte.Was du nach Modul 2 kannst: What you can do after Module 2
texte.Du beschreibst deinen Tag (*me levanto,: You describe your day (*me levanto, desayuno, salgo*), your home (*hay, está*), your likes (*me gusta*), what you can and must do (*puedo, tengo que*), and your plans (*voy a*). This lets you have a simple conversation about everyday life.
texte.conocer für Menschen, saber für Fakten: conocer for people, saber for facts
texte.*conocer* heißt „kennen“ im Sinne von sc: *conocer* means "to know" in the sense of having met: *Conozco a María*, *Conozco Madrid*. *saber* means "to know" or "to know how to": *Sé su nombre*, *Sé nadar*. When referring to people with *conocer*, always use an *a*.
texte.Beide sind in der ich-Form unregelmäßig: Both are irregular in the first person
texte.*conocer* wird zu *conozco* (mit z), *sa: *conocer* becomes *conozco* (with z), *saber* becomes *sé* (with an accent, to distinguish it from *se*). All other forms are regular: *conoces, conoce…* and *sabes, sabe…*
texte.*Me cae bien* heißt „er ist mir sympathi: *Me cae bien* means "I find him/her likable" – it's structured backwards. For people, use this instead of *me gusta*, because *me gusta Ana* sounds like you're in love. For more than one: *Me caen bien tus amigos.*
texte.Zwischen *no es simpático* und *es simpá: Between *no es simpático* and *es simpático*, there's a lot of room: *un poco* (a little, often used to soften negatives), *bastante* (quite), *muy* (very), *-ísimo* (extremely). *Es simpatiquísimo* is the strongest form – and very Spanish.
texte.Statt *es antipático* sagt man lieber *n: Instead of saying *es antipático*, it's better to say *no es muy simpático* or *es un poco especial*. Direct negative judgments about others are considered rude – the *un poco* softens the blow.
texte.Manche Adjektive haben keine weibliche F: Some adjectives don't have a feminine form
texte.Auf *-o* endende passen sich an: *tímido: Those ending in *-o* change: *tímido / tímida*. Those ending in *-e* or a consonant don't: *paciente*, *inteligente*, *joven* stay the same. An exception is those ending in *-or*: *trabajador* becomes *trabajadora*.
texte.*ser* für die dauerhafte Erscheinung: *E: *ser* for permanent appearance: *Es alto.* *tener* for body parts and their features: *Tiene el pelo largo.* *llevar* for removable things: *Lleva gafas y barba.* Master these three, and you won't make mistakes here.
texte.*bajo* wird zu *bajito*, *gordo* zu *gor: *bajo* becomes *bajito*, *gordo* becomes *gordito*, *viejo* becomes *viejecito*. The diminutive softens the word and sounds affectionate. Saying *Es bajita* is a loving description, while *Es baja* sounds neutral to cold.
texte.*Es guapa* heißt „sie ist hübsch“ – eine: *Es guapa* means "she is pretty" – a characteristic. *Está guapa* means "she looks pretty today" – a compliment for the moment. Use the second when going out, the first for someone not present.
texte.estar für Zustände, tener für Empfindung: Use estar for states, tener for sensations
texte.Mit *estar* beschreibst du eine Stimmung: With *estar*, you describe a mood: *estoy triste*, *está nervioso*. With *tener*, it's something you "have": *tengo miedo*, *tengo ganas*, *tengo sueño*. Rule of thumb: If it's an adjective, use *estar*; if it's a noun, use *tener*.
texte.echar de menos – vermissen mit vier Wört: echar de menos – missing someone with four words
texte.Das Spanische hat kein einzelnes Wort fü: Spanish doesn't have a single word for "miss": *Echo de menos a mi familia.* In Latin America, they say *extrañar*: *Extraño a mi familia.* Use *a* before people.
texte.*¿Estás bien?* ist die normale Frage. *¿: *¿Estás bien?* is the normal question. *¿Qué te pasa?* is more direct, meaning "what's wrong with you?" *¿Todo bien?* is the most casual. For all three, *Sí, es que estoy cansado* is a sufficient answer.
texte.*haber* + Partizip: *he, has, ha, hemos,: *haber* + past participle: *he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han* plus the form ending in *-ado* or *-ido*. For *-ar* verbs, use *-ado* (*hablar → hablado*), for *-er* and *-ir*, use *-ido* (*comer → comido*, *vivir → vivido*). Just two endings for all verbs.
texte.Zwischen *haber* und Partizip darf nicht: Nothing can come between *haber* and the participle: *No he comido todavía* – not *he no comido*. And the participle never changes: always *comido*, no matter who is speaking. Unlike in English, it doesn't move to the end.
texte.Zeitangaben, die das Perfekt verlangen: Time expressions that require the perfect tense
texte.In Spanien nimmt man das Perfekt für all: In Spain, the perfect tense is used for anything related to the current time: *hoy*, *esta semana*, *este año*, *ya*, *todavía no*, *nunca*. For completed actions like *ayer* or *el año pasado*, a different tense is used later.
texte.Die Ausnahmen im Perfekt: The exceptions in the perfect tense
texte.*hacer → hecho*, *decir → dicho*, *ver →: *hacer → hecho*, *decir → dicho*, *ver → visto*, *escribir → escrito*, *volver → vuelto*, *poner → puesto*, *abrir → abierto*, *romper → roto*. If you know these eight, you'll rarely stumble in everyday conversations.
texte.Was von einem unregelmäßigen Verb abgele: What is derived from an irregular verb remains irregular: *deshacer → deshecho*, *devolver → devuelto*, *descubrir → descubierto*. So, you're not just learning eight forms, but eight families.
texte.*¿Has estado alguna vez en…?* (Warst du: *¿Has estado alguna vez en…?* (Have you ever been to…?) and *Nunca he probado…* (I have never tried…) are the two sentences that drive any conversation about experiences. Both require the perfect tense.
texte.*hacer* für Sportarten ohne Ball: *hacer: *hacer* for sports without a ball: *hacer deporte*, *hacer yoga*. *jugar a* for games and ball sports: *jugar al tenis*, *jugar a las cartas* – the *a* is essential. *tocar* for instruments: *tocar el piano*, never *jugar*.
texte.*juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis,: *juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan* – the *u* changes to *ue*, except in *nosotros* and *vosotros*. The same pattern as *poder* and *volver*, just with a different vowel.
texte.*siempre* (immer), *a menudo* (oft), *a: *siempre* (always), *a menudo* (often), *a veces* (sometimes), *de vez en cuando* (occasionally), *casi nunca* (almost never), *nunca* (never). And with numbers: *tres veces por semana*, *dos veces al mes*.
texte.Vier Wege, eine Meinung zu sagen: Four ways to express an opinion
texte.*Creo que…* (ich glaube), *Me parece que: *Creo que…* (I believe), *Me parece que…* (it seems to me), *Pienso que…* (I think), *En mi opinión…* All four introduce the same idea. Important: After *que*, continue normally – *Creo que es buena*, not *Creo es buena*.
texte.*Me parece interesante* – wörtlich „es s: *Me parece interesante* – literally "it seems interesting to me." Like *gustar* and *doler*: *me parece*, *te parece*, *le parece*. For plurals: *Me parecen caras las entradas.* And as a question: *¿Qué te parece?* – What do you think?
texte.Ein nacktes *No* wirkt hart. Üblicher si: A plain *No* can sound harsh. More common are: *No estoy del todo de acuerdo* (not entirely), *Bueno, depende* (well, it depends), *Sí, pero…* When disagreeing, people often start with some agreement.
texte.Das Pronomen steht VOR dem Verb: *Lo leo: The pronoun goes BEFORE the verb: *Lo leo.* *La compro.* *Los veo.* When negating, it comes between *no* and the verb: *No lo entiendo.* Nothing else fits between the pronoun and the verb.
texte.Bei zwei Verben hast du die Wahl: *Lo vo: With two verbs, you have a choice: *Lo voy a buscar* or *Voy a buscarlo* – both are correct. For commands, it only goes at the end: *¡Cómpralo!* For negative commands, it's back in front: *¡No lo compres!*
texte.Es richtet sich nach dem Ding, nicht nac: It matches the object, not you
texte.*el libro* wird zu *lo*, *la carta* zu *: *el libro* becomes *lo*, *la carta* becomes *la*, *los zapatos* become *los*, *las llaves* become *las*. Ask yourself: What gender and number was the word I'm replacing? The pronoun matches that.
texte.Die Reihenfolge ist fest: erst das indir: The order is fixed: first the indirect object pronoun (*me, te, se, nos, os*), then the direct object pronoun (*lo, la, los, las*). *Me lo das* – you give it to me. Never *lo me das*. Both pronouns come before the verb.
texte.Träfen *le* und *lo* aufeinander, ergäbe: If *le* and *lo* were to meet, you'd get *le lo* – which is awkward to say. So, *le* changes to *se*: *Se lo doy* instead of *le lo doy*. The same rule applies with *les*: *Se lo mando a mis padres.*
texte.*Se lo doy* kann heißen: ich gebe es ihm: *Se lo doy* can mean: I give it to him, her, you, or them. If it's unclear, you can add: *Se lo doy a Ana.* The context usually clarifies who you mean.
texte.Statt *¿Quieres ir al cine?* klingt ein: Instead of *Do you want to go to the movies?*, a suggestion sounds nicer: *Why don't we go to the movies?* or *How about we go to the movies?* Both use the *we*-form – making you part of the plan.
texte.Erst Bedauern, dann Grund, dann Aussicht: First express regret, then give a reason, then offer an alternative: *I'd love to, but I have to work. How about another day?* A plain *I can't* can sound abrupt in Spain – the three steps are part of the etiquette.
texte.*Te invito* heißt nicht nur „ich lade di: *Te invito* means not only "I invite you," but also "I’ll cover it." Saying this and then wanting to split the bill can cause confusion. For just asking about availability, use *¿Vienes?* or *¿Te apuntas?*
texte.Der Ablauf eines Anrufs: The flow of a phone call
texte.*¿Dígame?* – *Hola, soy Tom. ¿Está Ana?*: *¿Dígame?* – *Hi, it's Tom. Is Ana there?* – *One moment, I'll get her.* Or: *She's not here right now, would you like to leave a message?* These four phrases cover almost every conversation.
texte.In Nachrichten fallen Wörter weg: *¿Nos: In messages, words get dropped: *¿Nos vemos?* instead of *¿Nos vemos hoy?*, *Voy* instead of *Ya voy para allá*. Common shortcuts: *xq* (porque), *tb* (también), *q* (que), *bss* (besos), *finde* (fin de semana).
texte.*No te oigo bien* (ich verstehe dich sch: *No te oigo bien* (I can't hear you well), *Se corta* (the connection is breaking up), *Te llamo luego* (I'll call you later), *Se me acaba la batería* (my battery is about to die). Four ways to exit any bad conversation.
texte.Verneint sieht der Befehl anders aus: Negating a command changes its form
texte.Der bejahte Befehl ist die *él*-Form: *¡: The affirmative command uses the *él* form: *¡Habla!* The negative swaps the vowel: *¡No hables!* For *-er* and *-ir* verbs, it's the opposite: *¡Come!* becomes *¡No comas!* Remember: The endings cross over.
texte.Bejaht hängt es hinten an: *¡Dímelo!* Ve: Affirmative, it attaches to the end: *¡Dímelo!* Negative, it goes in front: *¡No me lo digas!* Same rule as with modal verbs – in commands, it's not just the verb that matters, but also the *no*.
texte.Feste Wendungen lernt man als Ganzes: Learn fixed expressions as whole units
texte.*No te preocupes*, *No pasa nada*, *No m: *No te preocupes*, *No pasa nada*, *No me digas*, *Ten cuidado* – you say these a thousand times without thinking about how they're formed. Learn them as blocks, and the rules will follow naturally.
texte.Am weichsten: *Yo que tú…* (an deiner St: Softest: *Yo que tú…* (if I were you). Medium: *Deberías…* (you should). Strongest: *Tienes que…* (you must). And completely impersonal: *Hay que…* (one must) – this way, you give advice without addressing anyone directly.
texte.*Debes hablar con ella* klingt nach Anwe: *Debes hablar con ella* sounds like a command. *Deberías hablar con ella* sounds like advice. This *-ías* form is the conditional – it's worth memorizing the three most common: *deberías*, *podrías*, *sería*.
texte.Wer in Spanien ein Problem erzählt, beko: In Spain, when someone shares a problem, they get advice – unsolicited and from everyone present. It's not intrusive, it's showing interest. Just listening and saying nothing can seem indifferent.
texte.*Perdona* für Kleinigkeiten (jemanden an: *Perdona* for small things (like bumping into someone). *Lo siento* for genuine regret. *Lo siento mucho, de verdad* when it's serious. A simple *Perdón* is enough on the street, but not after an argument.
texte.Spanische Gespräche werden lauter, wenn: Spanish conversations get louder as they get more interesting – even among friends. If you're used to English norms, you might think it's an argument. The real warning sign isn't volume, it's silence.
texte.Der Ausweg aus jeder Spannung: The way out of any tension
texte.Drei Sätze lösen fast alles: *Tienes raz: Three phrases resolve almost anything: *Tienes razón* (you're right), *No era mi intención* (I didn't mean to), and *¿Lo olvidamos?* (shall we forget it?). They let you give in without anyone losing face.
texte.*Felicidades* passt fast immer. *Enhorab: *Felicidades* fits almost any occasion. *Enhorabuena* for achievements (exam, job, baby). *Feliz cumpleaños* only for birthdays. *Que te mejores* when someone is sick. And to toast: *¡Salud!*
texte.Um Mitternacht am 31. Dezember isst man: At midnight on December 31st, you eat one grape for each chime of the clock – twelve in twelve seconds. It's harder than it sounds, and that's exactly what makes it fun.
texte.Anders als in manchen Ländern packt man: Unlike in some countries, in Spain you open gifts right away, in front of the giver. It's customary to say something like *¡Qué bonito!* or *¡No tenías que molestarte!* – "you shouldn't have gone to the trouble."
texte.Dasselbe *nos* und *se* wie bei *me leva: The same *nos* and *se* used in *me levanto* mean "each other" in the plural: *Nos vemos* (we see each other), *Se escriben* (they write to each other). Only the plural forms can do this – it doesn't work with *me*.
texte.*Llevan tres años juntos* – sie sind sei: *Llevan tres años juntos* – they've been together for three years. *Llevo seis meses aquí* – I've been here for six months. *llevar* + time replaces the more cumbersome *desde hace*.
texte.Vorbeikommen statt verabreden: Dropping by instead of making plans
texte.Wer in Spanien Freunde treffen will, ruf: In Spain, if you want to meet friends, you call the same day. Planning three weeks ahead seems formal. A simple *¿Estás en casa? Me paso* is totally normal – even at nine in the evening.
texte.*¿Puedes…?* (kannst du), *¿Podrías…?* (k: *¿Puedes…?* (can you), *¿Podrías…?* (could you), *¿Te importaría…?* (would it bother you), *¿Sería posible…?* (would it be possible). The further down, the more polite – and more likely used with strangers.
texte.Beginn mit einer Entschuldigung, dann da: Start with an apology, then the issue, then the request: *Perdona que te moleste, es que se oye bastante. ¿Podrías bajarla un poco?* A direct *Haz menos ruido* makes you an enemy in the same building.
texte.Im Treppenhaus, im Aufzug, am Hauseingan: In the stairwell, in the elevator, at the entrance: You greet people. *Buenos días*, *Hola*, *Buenas*. Walking by silently is considered rude—even if you don't know each other.
texte.Der Einstieg ist immer derselbe: The opening is always the same
texte.*¿Qué tal?* – *Bien, ¿y tú?* – *Bien tam: *¿Qué tal?* – *Bien, ¿y tú?* – *Bien también.* Then comes the real question: *¿Y qué es de tu vida?* or *¿Cómo va el trabajo?* These three steps happen automatically and give you time to think.
texte.Kurze Wörter halten das Gespräch am Lebe: Short words keep the conversation alive
texte.*¿Ah sí?*, *Qué bien*, *Vaya*, *Claro*,: *¿Ah sí?*, *Qué bien*, *Vaya*, *Claro*, *Ya*, *Anda*. They don't say much but show interest. Not using them makes you seem uninterested—even if you're listening closely.
texte.Ein abruptes *Adiós* ist unhöflich. Übli: An abrupt *Adiós* is rude. The usual way is: *Bueno, te dejo, que tengo prisa. A ver si nos vemos pronto. ¡Un abrazo!* Three parts—announcement, hope, farewell.
texte.Einstieg: *Resulta que…* Verlauf: *Al pr: Beginning: *Resulta que…* Progression: *Al principio… luego… de repente…* Twist: *Total que…* Ending: *Al final… y ya está.* Using these four parts makes you sound like a natural storyteller.
texte.Menschen beschreiben (*es simpático, lle: Describing people (*es simpático, lleva gafas*), expressing feelings (*estoy nervioso, tengo ganas*), talking about today (*he hablado, he visto*), avoiding repetition (*se lo doy*), and having a conversation (*¿ah sí?, qué bien*).
texte.Erzählen zählt mehr als Fehlerfreiheit: Telling a story matters more than being error-free
texte.Niemand unterbricht dich wegen eines fal: No one interrupts you for a wrong article. But if you only answer with Yes or No, you won't be asked again. A mistake in a story is better than a perfect single sentence.
texte.*seguir* (weitergehen), *girar* (abbiege: *seguir* (to continue), *girar* (to turn), *cruzar* (to cross). Add the direction: *a la derecha* (to the right), *a la izquierda* (to the left), *todo recto* (straight ahead). That's almost all you need – *Sigues recto, giras a la derecha y cruzas la plaza.*
texte.*Está a diez minutos* (zehn Minuten entf: *Está a diez minutos* (ten minutes away), *a dos calles* (two blocks away), *a cien metros* (a hundred meters away). The *a* always marks the distance. And *andando* or *a pie* means you're walking.
texte.Spanier beschreiben Wege über sichtbare: Spaniards describe directions using visible things: *al lado del bar* (next to the bar), *enfrente de la farmacia* (in front of the pharmacy), *después del quiosco* (after the kiosk). You never hear compass directions. Ask for “north” and you'll get a shrug.
texte.Der Sie-Befehl tauscht den Vokal: The formal command swaps the vowel
texte.Bei *-ar*-Verben endet er auf *-e*: *hab: For *-ar* verbs, it ends in *-e*: *hablar → hable*, *girar → gire*. For *-er* and *-ir* verbs, it ends in *-a*: *comer → coma*, *seguir → siga*. It's the opposite of the usual ending – that's why it sounds wrong at first.
texte.Das Pronomen hängt hinten an: The pronoun sticks to the end
texte.Wie beim Du-Befehl: *Dígame* (sagen Sie: Like with the informal command: *Dígame* (tell me), *Perdóneme* (forgive me). In negative commands, it moves to the front: *No se preocupe* (don't worry), *No me lo diga* (don't tell me).
texte.Verstehen ist wichtiger als bilden: Understanding is more important than forming
texte.Diese Formen musst du vor allem *erkenne: You mainly need to *recognize* these forms: signs, announcements, and strangers on the street use them. You'll rarely need to say them yourself – *¿Puede decirme…?* is usually enough.
texte.en für Fahrzeuge, a für die eigenen Bein: en for vehicles, a for your own legs
texte.*ir en metro*, *en autobús*, *en tren*,: *ir en metro*, *en autobús*, *en tren*, *en coche*, *en bici*. But: *ir a pie* and *ir a caballo*. Rule of thumb: If you get in, use *en*; if you move yourself, use *a*.
texte.coger heißt nicht überall dasselbe: coger doesn't mean the same everywhere
texte.In Spanien ist *coger el metro* völlig n: In Spain, *coger el metro* is perfectly normal. In much of Latin America, *coger* is vulgar – there, they say *tomar el metro* or *agarrar*. A word that changes meaning across the Atlantic.
texte.*Billete sencillo* (Einzelfahrt), *ida y: *Billete sencillo* (single ticket), *ida y vuelta* (round trip), *abono mensual* (monthly pass), *validar* (validate), *andén* (platform), *dirección* (direction). These six words are all you need at any machine.
texte.Das Futur hörst du vor allem in Ansagen: You'll hear the future tense mostly in announcements
texte.Man hängt an den Infinitiv: *salir → sal: Add to the infinitive: *salir → saldrá*, *llegar → llegará*, *ser → será*. In daily life, people use *ir a* (*va a salir*), but announcements and schedules use this form. You need to recognize it, not form it.
texte.*Las diecinueve treinta* ist 19:30. Im G: *Las diecinueve treinta* is 19:30. In conversation, you'd say *las siete y media de la tarde* – but displays, tickets, and announcements use the long form. If you don't know it, you'll miss the train.
texte.Die vier Sätze jeder Durchsage: The four sentences of every announcement
texte.*El tren con destino a Sevilla…* (Ziel),: *El tren con destino a Sevilla…* (destination), *…efectuará su salida a las…* (departure), *…por la vía número…* (platform), *…lleva un retraso de…* (delay). Focus on the destination and numbers, you can ignore the rest.
texte.*No se puede aparcar* (man darf nicht) k: *No se puede aparcar* (you can't park) sounds straightforward. *Está prohibido aparcar* is the formal version you see on signs. *No aparque aquí* is the direct command. On signs, you'll mostly see the second form.
texte.*Se puede*, *se prohíbe*, *se habla espa: *Se puede*, *se prohíbe*, *se habla español*, *se vende* – this *se* refers to no one in particular, similar to the English 'one' or 'you'. It's on almost every sign in Spain.
texte.Weiße Parklinien: kostenlos. Blaue: gebü: White parking lines: free. Blue: paid, get a ticket. Green: residents only. Yellow: no stopping at all. Knowing the colors saves you from a *multa* (fine).
texte.Man hängt *-ía* an den Infinitiv: *quere: Add *-ía* to the infinitive: *querer → querría*, *gustar → gustaría*, *poder → podría*, *ser → sería*. *Quiero una habitación* is a demand, *Querría una habitación* is a request. One letter changes the tone.
texte.Die drei Formen, die du wirklich brauchs: The three forms you really need
texte.*querría* (ich hätte gern), *me gustaría: *querría* (I would like), *me gustaría* (I would like), *¿podría…?* (could you). These let you ask politely in any situation. Full conjugation can come later.
texte.Was an der Rezeption gefragt wird: What is asked at the reception
texte.*¿A nombre de quién?* (auf welchen Namen: *¿A nombre de quién?* (under what name), *¿Me deja su documento?* (ID please), *¿Cuántas noches?* (how many nights), *La salida es antes de las doce.* Four sentences that cover every check-in.
texte.Erst sachlich: *La ducha no funciona.* D: First, straightforward: *La ducha no funciona.* Then, request: *¿Podría arreglarlo?* Next, insist: *Llevo dos días esperando.* Finally: *¿Me trae el libro de reclamaciones?* The last step is rarely needed – but it works.
texte.Hotels, Restaurants und Läden müssen in: Hotels, restaurants, and shops in Spain must have a *libro de reclamaciones* (complaint book) and provide it upon request. The entry goes to the consumer authority. Just asking for it often solves the problem.
texte.Wer schreit, bekommt in Spanien seltener: In Spain, those who shout are less likely to get help than those who ask politely. *Perdona, es que llevo dos noches sin dormir. ¿Me podrías ayudar?* opens more doors than any demand – and keeps you welcome in the same place.
texte.*Se habla español*, *Se prohíbe fumar*,: *Se habla español*, *Se prohíbe fumar*, *Se ruega silencio*, *Se vende*. This *se* is like the English 'one' or 'you' in passive voice – no specific person is doing it. On signs, it's the norm; in conversation, you might say *you can't*.
texte.Einzahl oder Mehrzahl richtet sich nach: Singular or plural depends on the thing
texte.*Se vende casa* (ein Haus), *Se venden c: *Se vende casa* (one house), *Se venden casas* (several houses). The verb matches what is being sold – not the unknown seller. That's why you'll see both on signs.
texte.Die Tafel gilt, nicht die Durchsage: The board matters, not the announcement
texte.An spanischen Flughäfen wird kaum nament: At Spanish airports, names are rarely called, and gates can change last minute. Relying on announcements might leave you at the wrong gate. Checking the *pantalla* every twenty minutes is the safe way.
texte.Was gerade passiert ist, berichtest du i: When talking about something that just happened, use the present perfect: *Mi maleta no ha llegado.* *El vuelo se ha retrasado.* *Han perdido mi equipaje.* It fits perfectly – it happened today and still affects you.
texte.*Necesito un justificante por escrito* –: *Necesito un justificante por escrito* – no paperwork, no compensation. For luggage, the receipt is called *parte de irregularidad* or simply *PIR*. Without it, any future claim is hopeless.
texte.Ab drei Stunden Verspätung besteht meist: For delays over three hours, you usually have a right to compensation, and for over two hours, to refreshments. For lost luggage: report within 21 days. The magic phrase at the counter: *¿Tengo derecho a compensación?*
texte.*el más caro*, *la más bonita*, *los más: *el más caro*, *la más bonita*, *los más famosos*. If there's a noun, it goes in between: *el barrio más bonito*, not *el más bonito barrio*. And the comparison uses *de*: *el mejor de la ciudad*.
texte.Statt *muy bueno* sagt man *buenísimo*,: Instead of *muy bueno*, you say *buenísimo*, instead of *muy caro*, *carísimo*. Drop the final vowel and add *-ísimo*. It's not an exaggeration, just everyday language – Spaniards use it all the time.
texte.*bueno → el mejor*, *malo → el peor*, *g: *bueno → el mejor*, *malo → el peor*, *grande → el mayor*, *pequeño → el menor*. There's no *el más bueno*. For age: *mi hermano mayor* means older, not bigger.
texte.Wo das Deutsche zwischen der, die, das u: Where English distinguishes between who, which, and that, Spanish just uses *que*: *el hombre que vino*, *la casa que compré*, *los libros que leo*. No gender, no case – one of the few simplifications.
texte.donde für Orte, lo que für Sachverhalte: donde for places, lo que for situations
texte.*La plaza donde quedamos* (der Platz, wo: *La plaza donde quedamos* (the square where). *No entiendo lo que dices* (what you say) – *lo que* stands for something indefinite, not a specific thing. Both replace more cumbersome constructions.
texte.Anders als im Deutschen wird das Verb ni: Unlike in English, the verb doesn't get pushed to the end, and usually, no comma is needed: *El bar que está en la esquina es buenísimo.* The sentence just flows on.
texte.Die vier Fragen an jeder Kasse: The four questions at every ticket counter
texte.*¿A qué hora abren?* *¿Cuánto cuesta la: *¿A qué hora abren?* *¿Cuánto cuesta la entrada?* *¿Hay descuento para estudiantes?* *¿Cuándo es gratis?* These cover every attraction – the answers usually follow the same patterns.
texte.Der Prado ist ab 18 Uhr frei, der Reina: The Prado is free after 6 PM, the Reina Sofía after 7, and many city museums are free on Sundays. Asking *¿Hay alguna hora gratuita?* often saves you fifteen euros – you just need to ask.
texte.Auf Schildern steht *siglo XV*, gesproch: Signs say *siglo XV*, pronounced *siglo quince*. Remember: The 15th century is the 1400s. And many museums close on Mondays – a classic travel mistake.
texte.*Vamos a comer* (lass uns essen), *Podrí: *Vamos a comer* (let's eat), *Podríamos ir* (we could go), *¿Y si vamos…?* (what if we…). All three make you part of the plan. A *Quiero ir* would be a statement, not a suggestion.
texte.Zwischen 14 und 17 Uhr schließen viele L: Between 2 and 5 PM, many shops, churches, and smaller museums close. If you don't plan for these three hours, you'll find closed doors. That's exactly when the *siesta* is the perfect time to eat.
texte.*¿Nos da tiempo?* – schaffen wir das? An: *¿Nos da tiempo?* – Can we make it? Responses: *Vamos justos* (cutting it close), *Sobra tiempo* (plenty of time), *Ni de broma* (no way). Three phrases to simplify any planning.
texte.*Me duele desde hace dos días* – seit zw: *Me duele desde hace dos días* – for two days. Use *desde hace* with a duration. For a specific point in time, just use *desde*: *desde el lunes*, *desde ayer*. The doctor almost always asks this first.
texte.Der Ablauf ist immer gleich: The routine is always the same
texte.*¿Qué le pasa?* – *Me duele…* – *¿Desde: *¿Qué le pasa?* – *Me duele…* – *¿Desde cuándo?* – *Desde hace…* – *¿Es alérgico a algo?* – *Sí, a…* These five steps cover any initial consultation. You can show the rest if needed.
texte.Mit der Europäischen Krankenversicherung: With the European Health Insurance Card, you're treated like a local at public *centro de salud*. Without it, you pay upfront and claim later. Private clinics always bill directly.
texte.Eine Nummer für Polizei, Feuerwehr und R: One number for police, fire, and rescue across Europe. It works without credit, without a SIM card, and in Spain, it's often available in English. No need to remember more numbers.
texte.Die erste Frage ist immer *¿Dónde está u: The first question is always *¿Dónde está usted?* Give the street and house number or a nearby intersection before explaining what happened. This ensures help arrives even if the call drops.
texte.Nach einem Diebstahl brauchst du die *de: After a theft, you need the *denuncia* from the *comisaría* – without it, no insurance will pay. If you lose your passport, the consulate can help, but they also require the report first.
texte.Fremde Automaten fragen: *¿Acepta la com: Foreign ATMs might ask: *¿Acepta la comisión de 3,50 €?* If you press *Sí*, you pay. Even more costly is the question *¿Desea el cambio en euros?* – this “service” often adds a 5% fee. Always settle in the local currency.
texte.Viele Bars nehmen unter zehn Euro keine: Many bars don't accept cards for amounts under ten euros. *¿Tienes suelto?* is a common question. And if you try to pay for a coffee with a fifty, expect a *¿No tienes más pequeño?*
texte.*Lo pagamos a partes iguales* (zu gleich: *Lo pagamos a partes iguales* (equally), *a medias* (half and half), *cada uno lo suyo* (everyone pays their own). The last one is the least common in Spain – usually, one person pays and settles up later.
texte.Vor Adjektiven steht *tan … como*: *tan: Before adjectives, use *tan … como*: *tan caro como el hotel*. Before nouns and after verbs, use *tanto*: *tanto dinero como*, *No cuesta tanto como pensaba*. In negative, it's simply “less than.”
texte.*hotel* (klassisch), *hostal* oder *pens: *hotel* (classic), *hostal* or *pensión* (simpler, often family-run), *albergue* (dormitory-style hostel), *apartamento* (vacation rental with a kitchen). A *hostal* is not a hostel – that's also called *hostel* in Spanish.
texte.Die Herbergen des Jakobswegs: The hostels of the Camino de Santiago
texte.Entlang des *Camino de Santiago* gibt es: Along the *Camino de Santiago*, there's a dense network of *albergues* – often no reservation needed, first-come, first-served. Walkers have priority over cyclists, and you stay only one night.
texte.Grün: baden erlaubt. Gelb: Vorsicht, nur: Green: swimming allowed. Yellow: caution, only up to the waist. Red: no swimming at all – enforced with fines. A purple flag warns of jellyfish or pollution.
texte.hay que warnt ohne anzusprechen: hay que warns without addressing anyone
texte.*Hay que tener cuidado* – man muss aufpa: *Hay que tener cuidado* – you have to be careful. Unlike *ten cuidado*, it doesn't address anyone personally and sounds less instructive. This form is almost always used on signs.
texte.Zwischen 14 und 17 Uhr ist die Sonne in: Between 2 and 5 PM, the sun in Spain is dangerously strong in summer. Locals go to the beach in the morning or after five. If you're there at midday, you're definitely a tourist – and you'll be red by evening.
texte.*Llevo dos horas esperando* – ich warte: *Llevo dos horas esperando* – I've been waiting for two hours. *llevar* plus time plus verb ending in *-ando* or *-iendo*. This form sounds more factual than any complaint and is hard to argue against.
texte.Zahlen wirken: *Es la tercera vez*, *Lle: Numbers make an impact: *Es la tercera vez*, *Llevamos tres días*, *Pagué ochenta euros*. Stating facts gets you a solution more often than getting upset. In Spain, loudness is seen as losing control, not emphasis.
texte.Nach dem Nachdruck kommt das Angebot: *¿: After making your point, offer a solution: *¿Buscamos una solución?* This way, the other person can concede without losing face. And if they agree: *De acuerdo entonces, se lo agradezco.*
texte.*Suelo levantarme a las siete* – normale: *Suelo levantarme a las siete* – I usually get up at seven. *Soler* plus an infinitive means "usually" or "generally." It changes its stem: *suelo, sueles, suele, solemos, soléis, suelen*.
texte.Kastilisch spricht man überall. Dazu Kat: Castilian Spanish is spoken everywhere. Additionally, Catalan is spoken in Catalonia, Valencia, and the Balearic Islands, Galician in Galicia, and Basque in the Basque Country. Signs are bilingual there – no one expects you to know the second language.
texte.*Me llama la atención que…* (mir fällt a: *Me llama la atención que…* (I notice that) and *En Inglaterra, en cambio…* (on the other hand) describe without judging. Saying *Aquí lo hacen mal* closes doors – even if you mean it nicely.
texte.Anrede: *Querida Ana*. Ort und Lage: *Te: Greeting: *Querida Ana*. Place and situation: *Te escribo desde…* Highlights: *Lo mejor ha sido…, lo peor…* Closing: *Un abrazo*. This structure works for every postcard, message, and short report.
texte.Solange die Reise dauert, berichtest du: While your trip is ongoing, you report in the present perfect: *Hemos visitado tres ciudades.* Only when it's over and you're back home do you switch to the other past tense – that's covered in Module 5.
texte.Spanier schicken lieber *audios* als Tex: Spaniards prefer sending *audios* over texts – often several minutes long. For learners, this is a gift: real speaking pace, repeatable, and your response can be just as long.
texte.Was du nach Modul 4 kannst: What you can do after Module 4
texte.Nach dem Weg fragen und Antworten verste: Ask for directions and understand answers, book tickets and rooms, make complaints, visit a doctor, make an emergency call, and talk about your trip. That's everything a trip needs.
texte.Die Wendungen dieses Moduls funktioniere: The phrases in this module work from Mexico to Argentina. There are vocabulary differences – *coger* becomes *tomar*, *el móvil* becomes *el celular* – but the structure stays the same.
texte.*Me defiendo* heißt „ich komme zurecht“: *Me defiendo* means "I get by" – not perfectly, but independently. That's exactly what level A2 is: You solve your problems on your own, even if the sentences are a bit rough. Perfection comes later.
texte.Zwei Endungssätze statt drei: Two sets of endings instead of three
texte.Bei *-ar*: *-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -astei: For *-ar*: *-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron*. For both *-er* AND *-ir*: *-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron*. Unlike in the present tense, the second and third groups completely merge here.
texte.*hablo* (ich spreche) gegen *habló* (er: *hablo* (I speak) versus *habló* (he spoke). *hable* versus *hablé*. A single accent mark distinguishes between present and past – and between "I" and "he". When speaking, you hear it as emphasis at the end of the word.
texte.*hablamos* heißt „wir sprechen“ UND „wir: *hablamos* means "we speak" AND "we spoke", same with *vivimos*. Only context clarifies it: *Ayer hablamos* is past, *Hoy hablamos* is present. This doesn't happen with *-er*: *comemos* versus *comimos*.
texte.Diese Formen tragen keinen Akzent: These forms don't have an accent
texte.Regelmäßig heißt es *hablé*, *habló* – m: Regular forms are *hablé*, *habló* – with an accent. The irregular ones never do: *tuve*, *tuvo*, *hice*, *hizo*, *dije*, *dijo*. If the accent is missing, the verb is irregular. A reliable sign.
texte.*fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fue: *fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron* – the same set for both verbs. *Fui a Madrid* (I went) and *Fue difícil* (it was). You can't mix them up: After *ir* comes a place, after *ser* comes a description.
texte.*ser/ir → fui*, *hacer → hice*, *tener →: *ser/ir → fui*, *hacer → hice*, *tener → tuve*, *estar → estuve*, *poder → pude*, *decir → dije*, *venir → vine*, *dar → di*, *ver → vi*. You rarely need more to tell a story – the rest are regular.
texte.Die Zeitangabe wählt die Zeitform: The time expression chooses the tense
texte.Abgeschlossen und benannt → Indefinido:: Completed and named → Preterite: *ayer* (yesterday), *la semana pasada* (last week), *en 2020* (in 2020), *hace tres días* (three days ago). Still ongoing → Present Perfect: *hoy* (today), *esta semana* (this week), *este año* (this year). If you know the time expression, you don't have to think about the tense.
texte.*Hace tres días* – vor drei Tagen. *Hace: *Hace tres días* – three days ago. *Hace un año* – a year ago. Don't confuse it with *desde hace* ("for"): *Vivo aquí desde hace un año* means "for a year", *Vine hace un año* means "a year ago".
texte.*El otro día* kann vorgestern oder vor M: *El otro día* can mean the day before yesterday or months ago. *Hace un montón* means "ages ago". Precise time expressions can seem almost pedantic in conversation – when telling a story, you give a rough idea and move on.
texte.Gehört der Zeitraum noch zu heute?: Does the time period still include today?
texte.Ja → Perfekt: *hoy*, *esta semana*, *est: Yes → Present Perfect: *hoy* (today), *esta semana* (this week), *este año* (this year), *últimamente* (lately). No → Preterite: *ayer* (yesterday), *la semana pasada* (last week), *en 2019* (in 2019), *aquella vez* (that time). The only question is whether the time period is complete – not how long ago it was.
texte.Die Landkarte entscheidet mit: The map plays a role too
texte.Diese Regel gilt für Spanien. In Lateina: This rule applies to Spain. In Latin America, the Preterite is almost always used: *¿Ya comiste?* instead of *¿Ya has comido?* Both are correct – just don't mix them within a conversation.
texte.Warum das für Deutsche schwer ist: Why this is tricky for English speakers
texte.Im Deutschen sagt man „ich habe gegessen: In English, you say "I have eaten" for both. There's no choice between two forms, so you might not have a feel for it. The trick is not to rely on feeling, but to check the time reference.
texte.Zwei Endungssätze, keine Ausnahmen: Two sets of endings, no exceptions
texte.Bei *-ar*: *-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos,: For *-ar* verbs: *-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban*. For both *-er* and *-ir* verbs: *-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían*. No stem changes, no irregularities – the friendliest tense there is.
texte.*ser → era, eras, era, éramos, erais, er: *ser → era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran*. *ir → iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban*. *ver → veía, veías, veía…* That's it. All other verbs follow the rule, even those that are irregular in the present tense.
texte.Für Gewohnheiten (*Iba al colegio en bic: For habits (*Iba al colegio en bici*), for descriptions (*Era alto y llevaba gafas*), for age and time (*Tenía ocho años*, *Eran las tres*), and for states (*Estaba cansado*). It paints the background, not the action.
texte.Früher war alles anders: Back in the day, everything was different
texte.soler im Imperfekt für Gewohnheiten: Using 'soler' in the imperfect for habits
texte.*Solía ir al cine* – ich ging gewöhnlich: *Solía ir al cine* – I used to go to the movies. It says the same as *Iba al cine*, but emphasizes the regularity. In the imperfect, *soler* is regular: *solía, solías, solía, solíamos, solíais, solían*.
texte.Früher und heute nebeneinander: Then and now side by side
texte.Das Muster ist immer gleich: *Antes* plu: The pattern is always the same: *Antes* with the imperfect, *ahora* with the present. *Antes había un cine, ahora hay un supermercado.* *Antes íbamos andando, ahora vamos en coche.* One sentence, two tenses.
texte.*Cualquier tiempo pasado fue mejor* („je: *Cualquier tiempo pasado fue mejor* ("any past time was better") is often said sarcastically—about oneself or others who think everything was better in the past. If someone means it seriously, they usually face disagreement.
texte.Das Imperfekt baut die Bühne: Wetter, Or: The Imperfect sets the scene: weather, place, age, mood, what was happening. The Preterite brings the action: what happened next. *Era de noche y llovía* (setting). *Salí y cogí un taxi* (action).
texte.Läuft etwas und wird unterbrochen, steht: When something is ongoing and gets interrupted, the ongoing action is in the Imperfect and the interruption is in the Preterite: *Mientras cocinaba, sonó el teléfono.* *Cuando dormía, llamaron a la puerta.* The pattern is always the same.
texte.*sabía* (ich wusste) gegen *supe* (ich e: *sabía* (I knew) vs. *supe* (I found out). *conocía* (I knew) vs. *conocí* (I met). *quería* (I wanted) vs. *quise* (I tried). *podía* (I was able) vs. *pude* (I managed). Here, the form is not about style, but about meaning.
texte.Kulisse im Imperfekt: *Era de noche y ll: Backdrop in the Imperfect: *Era de noche y llovía.* Action in the Preterite: *Salí de casa.* Turning point: *De repente…* Resolution: *Al final…* Separating these four layers helps you automatically use the right tenses.
texte.*No te lo vas a creer…*, *Imagínate…*, *: *No te lo vas a creer…*, *Imagínate…*, *Resulta que…* – these phrases signal that something is coming. They aren't just decoration: they cue the listener to pay attention and ask questions.
texte.In Spanien wirft der Zuhörer ein: *¿En s: In Spain, listeners interject with: *¿En serio?*, *¡No me digas!*, *¿Y qué pasó?* If you listen silently, you seem bored. And storytellers expect this and pause for it.
texte.*lo mejor* (das Beste), *lo peor*, *lo m: *lo mejor* (the best), *lo peor*, *lo más interesante*, *lo difícil*. The *lo* turns an adjective into something you can discuss. And *lo que* introduces: *Lo que más me gustó fue…*
texte.Auf *¿Qué tal el viaje?* antwortet man k: To *¿Qué tal el viaje?* you reply briefly: a quick review, a highlight, done. *Great. What I liked most was the market.* If you talk for ten minutes, you'll lose your audience – let them ask questions instead.
texte.Statt *Fue horrible* sagt man *Esperaba: Instead of *It was horrible*, say *I expected more* or *It wasn't bad, but…* This sounds like an assessment rather than a complaint – and leaves room for others to have a different opinion.
texte.*Rompí el vaso* heißt „ich zerbrach das: *Rompí el vaso* means “I broke the glass” – my fault. *Se me rompió el vaso* means “the glass broke on me” – it just happened. Spanish has a special form for mishaps that doesn't blame anyone.
texte.*Se me cayó el móvil* (eines) gegen *Se: *Se me cayó el móvil* (one) versus *Se me cayeron las llaves* (several). You aren't the subject, the object is – so the verb matches the object, not you. Just like with *gustar* and *doler*.
texte.*se me*, *se te*, *se le*, *se nos*, *se: *se me*, *se te*, *se le*, *se nos*, *se les*. *¿Se te olvidó?* (did you forget?), *Se nos hizo tarde* (we got late). The *se* stays, only the pronoun after it changes.
texte.Bei *-ar* endet es auf *-ando*: *habland: For *-ar* verbs, it ends in *-ando*: *hablando*. For *-er* and *-ir* verbs, it ends in *-iendo*: *comiendo*, *viviendo*. Place *estar* in the appropriate tense before it: *estoy comiendo*, *estaba comiendo*, *estuve comiendo*.
texte.*I am working here* heißt auf Spanisch *: *I am working here* in Spanish is *Trabajo aquí*, not *Estoy trabajando aquí*. The continuous form indicates an action happening right now. For habits and ongoing states, use the simple form.
texte.*Sigo estudiando* – ich lerne weiter. *L: *Sigo estudiando* – I keep studying. *Llevo dos horas esperando* – I have been waiting for two hours. The gerund can also follow other verbs to express continuity.
texte.haber im Imperfekt plus Partizip: haber in the Imperfect plus Past Participle
texte.*había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais: *había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían* plus the same participle form as in the Perfect: *hablado*, *comido*, *hecho*, *visto*. If you know the Perfect, you can use this form right away – only the first part changes.
texte.Es markiert, was VOR dem Erzählten gesch: It marks what happened BEFORE the story: *Cuando llegué, ya había salido.* He left first, then I arrived. Without this form, you'd have to explain awkwardly what happened first.
texte.„Als ich ankam, war er schon gegangen\": "When I arrived, he had already left" – same structure, same logic. After dealing with the Preterite and Imperfect, which don't exist in English, this is a relief: Here, you can translate directly.
texte.Die Zeit rutscht eine Stufe zurück: The tense shifts back one level
texte.Aus *„Vengo mañana\"* wird *Dijo que ven: In Spanish, *„Vengo mañana"* becomes *Dijo que venía al día siguiente*. Present tense shifts to imperfect, perfect and simple past become pluperfect, and future becomes conditional. Just like in English, everything moves one step back in time.
texte.Fragen mit si oder Fragewort: Questions with if or question word
texte.Ja-Nein-Fragen bekommen *si*: *„¿Vienes?: Yes-no questions use *if*: *„Are you coming?"* becomes *He asked if I was coming*. Questions with a question word keep it: *„Where do you live?"* becomes *He asked where I lived* – the accent remains, even though there's no question mark anymore.
texte.*o eso dijo* (so sagte er jedenfalls), *: *o eso dijo* (or so he said), *según él* (according to him), *al parecer* (apparently). These phrases let you relay information without committing to it – useful when you're not sure if it's true.
texte.Endet das Wort auf *-o* oder *-a*, tausc: If a word ends in *-o* or *-a*, swap the vowel: *momento → momentito*, *casa → casita*. If it ends in *-e*, *-n*, or *-r*, add *-cito*: *coche → cochecito*, *joven → jovencito*, *mujer → mujercita*.
texte.*Un momentito* ist nicht kürzer als ein: *Un momentito* isn't shorter than a moment, *un cafecito* isn't smaller. The form makes the sentence friendlier, more pleasant, warmer. That's why you hear it often in requests: *¿Me das un poquito de agua?*
texte.Dort wird noch häufiger verkleinert – *a: Diminutives are even more common there – *ahorita* (soon), *tantito* (a little bit), *cerquita* (very close). In Mexico, *ahorita* can mean anything from right now to later today.
texte.Zwei Verben, ein Sinn – zwei Bauweisen: Two verbs, one meaning – two constructions
