texte.*acordarse* braucht *se* und *de*: *Me a: *acordarse* needs *se* and *de*: *Me acuerdo de ti.* *recordar* doesn't need either: *Te recuerdo.* Both mean "to remember"; *acordarse* is the everyday form, *recordar* sounds a bit more formal.
texte.Zwischen „ich weiß es“ und „keine Ahnung: Between "I know it" and "no idea" lies *me suena*: it sounds familiar, but I can't quite place it. Very common – and more polite than a flat *No sé*.
texte.*¿Te acuerdas de cuando…?* eröffnet ein: *¿Te acuerdas de cuando…?* opens up a shared conversation. Unlike a factual question, it invites elaboration – and that's exactly the point. Short answers can seem dismissive here.
texte.al plus Infinitiv verknüpft zwei Ereigni: al plus infinitive links two events
texte.*Al terminar la carrera, se mudó* – als: *Al terminar la carrera, se mudó* – upon finishing his studies, he moved. Shorter than *Cuando terminó…* and typical for storytelling. It works with any verb: *al llegar*, *al salir*, *al verla*.
texte.*Nació en… se crió en… estudió… se mudó: *Nació en… se crió en… estudió… se mudó a… trabajó como… desde entonces…* These six building blocks support any life story, whether it's your own or that of a famous person.
texte.*mil novecientos noventa* (1990), *dos m: *mil novecientos noventa* (1990), *dos mil diez* (2010), *dos mil veintitrés* (2023). Unlike in English, you don't say "nineteen hundred," but count in thousands. And "in the year" is simply *en*.
texte.*¡Qué* + Adjektiv oder Substantiv: *¡Qué: *¡Qué* + adjective or noun: *¡Qué bien!*, *¡Qué día!* *¡Menudo* + noun, always adjusted: *¡Menudo susto!*, *¡Menuda suerte!* *¡Vaya* + noun: *¡Vaya día!* All three express the same amazement.
texte.*¡Menuda suerte!* heißt echt „was für ei: *¡Menuda suerte!* means "what luck" – or sarcastically, the opposite. *Para variar* ("for a change") is almost always ironic: *Llegó tarde, para variar.* The tone, not the words, makes the meaning.
texte.Wer eine Geschichte hört und nur nickt,: If you listen to a story and just nod, you might seem uninterested. Interjections are expected: *¿En serio?*, *¡No me digas!*, *¡Qué fuerte!*, *¿Y qué pasó?* The storyteller even pauses for them.
texte.Das Imperfekt malt, das Indefinido beweg: The Imperfect paints, the Preterite moves
texte.Märchen zeigen den Unterschied am reinst: Fairy tales show the difference clearly: *Érase una vez un rey que tenía tres hijas* (setting, Imperfect). *Un día, el rey llamó a la mayor* (action, Preterite). Reading fairy tales helps you practice both tenses.
texte.*Érase una vez* ist altes Spanisch und w: *Érase una vez* is old Spanish and is only used in this phrase today. You don't analyze it, you learn it as a block – just like "once upon a time" isn't broken down grammatically.
texte.*Y colorín colorado, este cuento se ha a: *Y colorín colorado, este cuento se ha acabado* – the words don't mean much, they just rhyme. Every Spanish-speaking child knows this phrase. It's the equivalent of "and they lived happily ever after."
texte.Von fast sicher bis reine Ahnung: From almost certain to just a guess
texte.*Tuvo que ser* (es muss gewesen sein, fa: *Tuvo que ser* (it must have been, almost certain), *debía de ser* (it was probably), *seguramente* (surely), *supongo que* (I suppose), *a lo mejor* and *igual* (maybe), *quién sabe* (who knows). Six levels for the same uncertainty.
texte.Streng genommen: *debe de estar* = er is: Strictly speaking: *debe de estar* = he is probably there (assumption), *debe estar* = he must be there (obligation). In spoken Spanish, the *de* often drops, and context clarifies it. You need to understand both, but using the assumption is enough.
texte.*Igual viene mañana* bedeutet „vielleich: *Igual viene mañana* means "maybe he'll come tomorrow" – not "he's coming right away". This meaning is very Spanish and reliably confuses learners. In Latin America, they might say *capaz que* instead.
texte.*desde* markiert den Anfangspunkt: *desd: *desde* marks the starting point: *desde marzo*. *hasta* marks the end: *hasta las once*. *durante* covers the whole duration: *durante tres años*. And *desde hace* indicates the length of time instead of a point: *desde hace tres años*.
texte.llevar ist die spanischste Lösung: llevar is the most Spanish solution
texte.*¿Cuánto llevas aquí?* – *Llevo seis mes: *¿Cuánto llevas aquí?* – *Llevo seis meses.* No *desde*, no *hace*, just *llevar* plus time. This is the form you hear in everyday conversation; all others sound awkward.
texte.tardar heißt brauchen, nicht dauern: tardar means to take time, not to last
texte.*Tardé dos horas en llegar* – ich brauch: *Tardé dos horas en llegar* – I took two hours. For "it lasts" you use *durar*: *La película dura dos horas.* One refers to the person, the other to the thing.
texte.dar und hacer als Gefühlsverben: dar and hacer as emotion verbs
texte.*dar* für Unangenehmes: *me dio pena, mi: *dar* for unpleasant feelings: *me dio pena, miedo, rabia, vergüenza*. *hacer* for pleasant ones: *me hizo ilusión, gracia*. Both work like *gustar* – it's not you feeling it, but the thing doing it to you.
texte.Zwei Wendungen ohne deutsches Gegenstück: Two expressions without an English equivalent
texte.*Me hizo ilusión* meint Vorfreude und Rü: *Me hizo ilusión* combines anticipation and emotion – "I was happy" only captures part of it. *Me hace gracia* means "I find it funny", not "it gives me grace". Learn both as fixed expressions.
texte.sentar bien – vom Essen zum Gefühl: sentar bien – from food to feeling
texte.*Me sentó mal la comida* heißt „das Esse: *Me sentó mal la comida* means "the food didn't agree with me." The same verb is used for feeling hurt: *Me sentó mal su comentario.* Whether it's food or a comment, it's about what doesn't sit well with you.
texte.*Imperfekt* malt die Kulisse (*era de no: *Imperfect* sets the scene (*era de noche*). *Preterite* moves the action (*salí*). *Pluperfect* explains what happened before (*ya había cerrado*). *Present Perfect* connects to now (*nunca he vuelto*). Separate them to tell a clear story.
texte.Was du nach Modul 5 kannst: What you can do after Module 5
texte.Von gestern und von damals erzählen, Mis: Talk about past events and mishaps, report speech, express assumptions, name feelings about experiences, and maintain a story for several minutes. This is the leap from A2 to B1.
texte.Nicht am Wortschatz – den bekommt man ge: Not by vocabulary – that's given to you. But by whether someone can distinguish *era* from *fue*. If you can do that, people in Spain won't slow down their speech for you. That's the real threshold.
texte.Ein Land, das keins ist: A country that's not just one
texte.Zwischen Galicien und Andalusien liegen: Between Galicia and Andalusia, there are different languages, climates, cuisines, and festivals. When people say "typical Spanish," they often mean Andalusia – flamenco and bullfighting are almost as foreign in the north as they are in England.
texte.Jede hat eigenes Parlament, eigene Bildu: Each has its own parliament, education, and health policies. That's why school holidays, public holidays, and even store hours vary from region to region – there's no uniform Spain in daily life.
texte.*La España verde* nennt man den Norden –: The north is called *La España verde* – Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, Basque Country. It rains more there than in London, the landscape is reminiscent of Ireland, and no one goes to the beach in August.
texte.Fällt ein Feiertag auf Dienstag oder Don: If a holiday falls on a Tuesday or Thursday, people take the day in between off – that's the *puente*, the bridge. When there are two holidays in a week, it's called an *acueducto*. Half of Spain plans their year around this.
texte.Bei den *Fallas* in Valencia werden mete: During the *Fallas* in Valencia, towering figures are built – and on the last night, they're all set on fire. A year of work for one night. The same principle applies to the bonfires on June 24th.
texte.Jede Region hat eigene Feiertage: Every region has its own holidays
texte.Neben den nationalen gibt es regionale u: Besides national holidays, there are regional and city-specific ones. If you work in Madrid and live in Toledo, you have two different calendars. Hence the everyday question: *¿Aquí es festivo mañana?*
texte.Nach *ojalá* steht nicht *viene*, sonder: After *ojalá*, you don't use *viene*, but *venga*. Not *es*, but *sea*. You already know these forms – from the formal command: *venga*, *sea*, *tenga*. It's the same form, just used differently: the Subjunctive.
texte.Der Indikativ berichtet, was ist: *Luis: The Indicative states what is: *Luis viene.* The Subjunctive keeps things uncertain: *Ojalá venga Luis.* It's not certain, it's just a wish. This distinction isn't common in English, so it's something new to learn.
texte.*Ojalá* stammt von *law šāʾ Allāh* – „so: *Ojalá* comes from *law šāʾ Allāh* – "if God wills." Around four thousand Spanish words come from Arabic: *almohada* (pillow), *aceite* (oil), *azúcar* (sugar), *alcalde* (mayor). They're often recognizable by the *al-* at the start.
texte.Vom ich-Stamm, dann Vokal tauschen: Start with the 'yo' form, then swap the vowel
texte.Nimm die *yo*-Form im Präsens, streiche: Take the *yo* form in the present tense, drop the *-o* and swap the vowel: *hablo → hable*, *como → coma*, *vivo → viva*. For *-ar* verbs, use *e*, and for *-er* and *-ir* verbs, use *a*. It's the opposite of the usual ending.
texte.Weil man vom *yo*-Stamm ausgeht, wandern: Since you start with the *yo* form, any irregularities carry over: *tengo → tenga*, *vengo → venga*, *hago → haga*, *digo → diga*, *conozco → conozca*. If you know the *yo* form, you know the subjunctive.
texte.*ser → sea*, *estar → esté*, *ir → vaya*: *ser → sea*, *estar → esté*, *ir → vaya*, *saber → sepa*, *haber → haya*, *dar → dé*. They don't follow the rule because their *yo* form doesn't end in *-o*. Exactly six of them – and you need all six daily.
texte.Der Subjuntivo braucht einen Wechsel: IC: The subjunctive needs a change: I am happy that YOU are coming – *Me alegro de que vengas.* If it's the same person, use the infinitive: *Me alegro de venir.* No change, no subjunctive.
texte.Alles, was bewertet statt berichtet, ver: Anything that evaluates instead of reports requires it: *me alegro de que*, *es una pena que*, *es normal que*, *me molesta que*. The subordinate clause doesn't state a fact but what the feeling is about.
texte.Im Deutschen heißt es „ich freue mich, d: In English, we say "I'm happy that you're coming" – no difference from "I know that you're coming." Spanish separates the two: Knowing is indicative, feeling is subjunctive. You need to learn the rule because the intuition isn't there.
texte.Norden: Fisch, Eintöpfe, Sauerrahm. Zent: North: fish, stews, sour cream. Center: oven-baked meats, legumes. South: cold soups, fried foods, lots of olive oil. Levante: rice. Ask about "Spanish cuisine" and you'll get four different answers.
texte.Die valencianische Original-Paella enthä: The original Valencian paella contains rabbit, chicken, and green beans – no seafood. The version with shrimp is called *paella de marisco*. Adding chorizo is considered sacrilege in Valencia, and they'll let you know.
texte.*Gazpacho* nur im Sommer, *cocido* nur i: *Gazpacho* only in summer, *cocido* only in winter, *calçots* only from January to March. Seasonality isn't a trend, it's a given – asking for stew in August just seems odd.
texte.Man bleibt nicht sitzen: eine Tapa, ein: You don't stay put: one tapa, one drink, then on to the next bar. Three to five stops are normal. Spending the whole evening in one place isn't tapear, it's having dinner.
texte.In Granada, León und Almería kommt die T: In Granada, León, and Almería, the tapa comes free with your drink, and you often can't choose it. In Madrid, Barcelona, and Valencia, you pay for it. Not knowing this might leave you puzzled by the bill.
texte.*Tapa* ist ein Häppchen, *media ración*: *Tapa* is a small bite, *media ración* is a small plate, *ración* is a large one to share. For four people, order three to four *raciones* – everything goes in the middle.
texte.*Creo que viene* – ich glaube es, also b: *Creo que viene* – I believe it, so I report it. *No creo que venga* – I don't believe it, so it's uncertain. The same goes for *es verdad que* versus *no es verdad que*, *me parece que* versus *no me parece que*."
texte.*dudo que*, *puede que*, *es posible que: *dudo que*, *puede que*, *es posible que*, *no estoy seguro de que* – these phrases use the Subjunctive even without negation. The verb itself already expresses uncertainty, so no additional negation is needed.
texte.Ein *No lo veo así* ist kein Affront. Sp: A *No lo veo así* isn't offensive. Spanish conversations thrive on differing opinions – agreeing with everything can seem dull. Just soften the start: *En parte tienes razón, pero…*
texte.Der wichtigste Unterschied: das c: The most important difference: the c
texte.In Spanien klingt *c* vor *e* und *i* wi: In Spain, *c* before *e* and *i* sounds like the English "th": *cinco*, *gracias*. Throughout the Americas, it sounds like an *s*: *sinco*, *grasias*. This is called *seseo*, and it affects more speakers than the Spanish variant.
texte.Zu einer Gruppe sagt man in Amerika imme: In the Americas, you always use *ustedes* for a group – even with friends. The *vosotros* forms are understood but never used. If you're only traveling in the Americas, you can skip these six forms.
texte.Kein Dialekt ist der richtige: No dialect is the correct one
texte.Mexiko hat mehr Spanischsprecher als Spa: Mexico has more Spanish speakers than Spain and Argentina combined. "Pure Spanish" is a myth – each region considers its version the clearest. What's important is being understood, not where you're from.
texte.*Coger el autobús* ist in Spanien völlig: *Coger el autobús* is perfectly normal in Spain. In Argentina, Mexico, Chile, and Uruguay, *coger* is vulgar. There, you say *tomar* or *agarrar*. This is the most important vocabulary of this lesson.
texte.In Mexiko kann *ahorita* alles von „sofo: In Mexico, *ahorita* can mean anything from "right now" to "later today" – or not at all. *Ahorita voy* often means: sometime. If you want to be precise, say *ya voy* or give a specific time.
texte.Du musst dich nicht entscheiden. Alle ve: You don't have to decide. Everyone understands both versions – a Spaniard knows what *celular* is, a Mexican knows *móvil*. Only with *coger* is it worth using the safer form.
texte.Die Betonung wandert nach hinten: The emphasis shifts to the end
texte.Aus *tú hablas* wird *vos hablás*, aus *: *Tú hablas* becomes *vos hablás*, *tú tienes* becomes *vos tenés*, *tú puedes* becomes *vos podés*. The ending carries the accent, and the stem change is dropped: not *tienes*, but *tenés*.
texte.Argentinien, Uruguay und Paraguay durchg: Argentina, Uruguay, and Paraguay consistently. Large parts of Central America too. In Colombia and Chile, it mixes with *tú*. In Spain, Mexico, and Peru, there's no *voseo*.
texte.Niemand erwartet von Lernenden, dass sie: No one expects learners to use *vos*. But if you listen to Argentine music or watch shows, you'll encounter it often. Recognizing it is enough – and everyone there understands *tú* too.
texte.*Estar como una cabra* – nie *como una v: *Estar como una cabra* – never *como una vaca*. *Meter la pata* – never *meter el pie*. You can't swap words, even if it seems logical. That's why you learn them as a block, not as grammar.
texte.Fünf sicher eingesetzte Wendungen wirken: Five well-used idioms are better than twenty half-understood ones. Using them in the wrong place makes you sound like a walking language course. When in doubt: speak normally.
texte.Viele Wendungen gelten nur in Spanien. *: Many expressions are specific to Spain. *Estar como una cabra* is understood in Mexico but not used. Conversely, they say *estar bien loco* there. Idioms are the most regional part of a language.
texte.In Spanien wird beim Essen über Essen ge: In Spain, people talk about food while eating – yesterday's, tomorrow's, and what's currently being served. It's no surprise the language is full of culinary imagery. Understanding these expressions means hearing more than just words.
texte.Kürbisse galten im Mittelalter als Mitte: In the Middle Ages, pumpkins were seen as a remedy against desire – if you received one, you got the message. Today, *dar calabazas* simply means "to reject someone." Few know the origin, but everyone knows the phrase.
texte.mala leche ist stärker als es klingt: mala leche is stronger than it sounds
texte.*Estar de mala leche* heißt schlechte La: *Estar de mala leche* means to be in a bad mood. *Tener mala leche*, on the other hand, means to be malicious – a real accusation. One word difference, two very different meanings.
texte.Im Laden, im Café, unter Kollegen, oft s: In shops, cafes, among colleagues, and often even at the doctor's: *tú*. The formal 'you' is used with significantly older people, in official settings, and at very formal occasions. Someone from an English-speaking country might use the formal 'you' too much here.
texte.In Kolumbien, Costa Rica und Teilen Mexi: In Colombia, Costa Rica, and parts of Mexico, *usted* is common – sometimes even between spouses. Bringing the same casualness as in Madrid can quickly come off as disrespectful.
texte.*Don* und *doña* stehen vor dem VORNAMEN: *Don* and *doña* are used before the FIRST NAME: *don Carlos*, *doña María*. They express respectful familiarity – the boss is called *don Carlos*, not *Mr. Carlos*. With last names, you say *el señor García*.
texte.Er entstand im 18. Jahrhundert aus der K: It originated in the 18th century from the culture of the Roma in Andalusia. In northern Spain, it has no roots – there are bagpipes in Galicia and unique dances in the Basque Country. There's as little "Spanish music" as there is Spanish cuisine.
texte.Salsa, Merengue, Bachata und Reggaetón k: Salsa, Merengue, Bachata, and Reggaetón come from Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Puerto Rico. Today, you hear this music in Madrid more often than Flamenco – and for learners, it's better practice.
texte.Songtexte wiederholen sich, reimen sich: Song lyrics repeat, rhyme, and stick in your mind. Singing along with the chorus helps you practice pronunciation and rhythm at the same time. Reggaetón is often easier than Flamenco – the Cante is hard to understand even for Spaniards.
texte.Römer (200 v. Chr. bis 400), Westgoten,: Romans (200 BC to 400 AD), Visigoths, Arabs (711 to 1492), then the Christian kingdom. Each layer left traces in language and architecture – that's why there's a cathedral inside a mosque in Córdoba.
texte.Im selben Jahr fiel Granada, wurden Jude: In the same year, Granada fell, Jews and later Muslims were expelled, and Columbus reached America. For Spain, it was a founding year, for many others the start of violence and loss. Both are part of the story.
texte.Bürgerkrieg und Franco-Diktatur sind nic: The Civil War and Franco's dictatorship are not just history, but family history – grandparents lived through them. Questions are okay, but judgments are best avoided. The same goes for the independence movements in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
texte.Nicht Freitag der 13., sondern *martes t: Not Friday the 13th, but *martes trece*. The saying goes: *En martes, ni te cases ni te embarques* – on Tuesdays, neither marry nor embark on a journey. The same day is considered unlucky in Greece and Italy.
texte.Traditionell bringen nicht der Weihnacht: Traditionally, it's not Santa Claus but the Three Wise Men who bring gifts – on the morning of January 6th. Children leave out shoes and water for the camels the night before. Santa Claus was a later addition.
texte.Wer beim Anstoßen ein Glas Wasser hebt,: If you toast with a glass of water, it's said to bring bad luck to the group. If you don't drink, it's better not to raise a glass at all. It might sound silly, but it's taken seriously – and easy to avoid.
texte.*¿Cómo se dice…?* und *¿Qué significa…?*: *¿Cómo se dice…?* and *¿Qué significa…?* are not interruptions, but compliments: you're showing interest. Almost everyone enjoys explaining – and many will ask you how to say it in English.
texte.Spanier überhören Fehler höflich, statt: Spaniards politely overlook mistakes instead of pointing them out. If you want to be corrected, you have to ask: *Corrígeme, por favor.* Otherwise, you might speak with the same mistakes for years without realizing it.
texte.*Me defiendo* (ich komme zurecht), *me c: *Me defiendo* (I get by), *me cuesta* (it's hard for me), *ya me sale solo* (it comes naturally), *estoy aprendiendo*. These phrases help you describe your level without putting yourself down – *mi español es malo* usually isn't true.
texte.Zwischen A1 und A2 geht es schnell, dana: Between A1 and A2, progress feels fast, but then it seems to stall. Don't be fooled: Progress shifts from vocabulary to nuances. You'll notice it when you have a conversation that seemed impossible three months ago.
texte.Ab B1 lernt man außerhalb des Kurses: From B1, learning happens outside the classroom
texte.Serien im Original, Podcasts, Musik, Büc: Original series, podcasts, music, books, real conversations. A course can provide structure, but the amount of language you need from here on can't fit into a single lesson.
texte.Zwanzig Minuten Gespräch bringen mehr al: Twenty minutes of conversation is worth more than two hours of vocabulary study—because you realize what's missing. *Intercambios* are available in most big cities: One hour of Spanish, one hour of English, both benefit.
texte.Nach Wunsch (*ojalá*, *espero que*), nac: With wishes (*ojalá*, *espero que*), feelings and judgments (*me alegro de que*, *es raro que*), doubt (*dudo que*, *puede que*), and negative opinions (*no creo que*). Four triggers—know them, and you'll usually get the form right.
texte.Was du nach Modul 6 kannst: What you can do after Module 6
texte.Über Regionen, Feste und Küche sprechen,: Talk about regions, festivals, and cuisine, express and doubt opinions, name cultural differences without judging, understand idioms, and avoid major pitfalls between Spain and Latin America.
texte.Eine zweite Sortierung der Welt: A second way to sort the world
texte.Spanisch trennt *ser* und *estar*, wo De: Spanish separates *ser* and *estar*, where English just uses "to be." It distinguishes fact from possibility, where we might use the same words. Learning this gives you not just vocabulary, but distinctions that were previously invisible.
texte.Was machst du beruflich?: What do you do for a living?
texte.*¿A qué te dedicas?* – wörtlich „womit b: *¿A qué te dedicas?* – literally "what do you dedicate yourself to?" This is the usual form, not *¿Qué eres?* And keep the answer short: *Trabajo en un banco.* Explaining your position for minutes seems pretentious.
texte.In Spanien unterscheidet man scharf zwis: In Spain, there's a clear distinction between *contrato fijo* (permanent), *temporal* (temporary), and *por obra* (project-based). Saying *fijo* also hints at your life situation – temporary contracts are common.
texte.Wer selbständig arbeitet, meldet sich al: If you work independently, you register as an *autónomo* and pay a fixed monthly fee – regardless of your earnings. Hence the common complaint: *La cuota de autónomos es un robo.*
texte.Beides war lange üblich und gilt heute a: Both were common for a long time but are now seen as problematic. Asking for a photo stands out. Marital status and nationality are also out – just name, contact, education, experience, skills.
texte.Die jüngste Station steht oben. Bei jede: The most recent position goes on top. For each job: period, company, position, then two to three lines about the *funciones*. Use past tense verbs: *me encargaba de*, *coordiné*, *desarrollé*.
texte.Statt „gut\" oder „fließend\" schreibt m: Instead of "good" or "fluent," use A1 to C2. *Español: B1*, *Inglés: C1*. Writing *nativo* means native speaker. And *nociones* means basic knowledge – more honest than an inflated B2.
texte.Erstens: Warum ich schreibe (*En respues: First: Why I'm writing (*En respuesta a su anuncio…*). Second: What I bring. Third: Why this company. Fourth: Availability and closing. No one reads more than one page.
texte.Im formellen Spanisch folgt auf *Estimad: In formal Spanish, after *Estimados señores* you use a colon, not a comma – and the next word is capitalized. At the end, you use *Atentamente* or *Un cordial saludo*, not a literal translation of English closings.
texte.*Considero que encajo en el perfil* ist: *Considero que encajo en el perfil* is confident and appropriate. *Sería un honor* sounds exaggerated, *quiero el trabajo* is too direct. The Spanish tone is balanced – factual with a touch of warmth.
texte.Fünf Fragen, die immer kommen: Five questions that always come up
texte.*Háblame de ti.* *¿Por qué esta empresa?: *Háblame de ti.* *¿Por qué esta empresa?* *¿Cuáles son tus puntos fuertes y débiles?* *¿Dónde te ves en cinco años?* *¿Tienes alguna pregunta?* Prepare these five, and you're ready for eighty percent of the interview.
texte.Ein *soy demasiado perfeccionista* gilt: Saying *soy demasiado perfeccionista* is considered cliché. Better: mention a real weakness and what you're doing about it. *Me cuesta delegar, por eso ahora reparto tareas desde el principio.*
texte.Auf *¿Tienes alguna pregunta?* mit „nein: Answering *¿Tienes alguna pregunta?* with "no" seems uninterested. Two good questions: *¿Cómo es un día normal en el puesto?* and *¿Qué esperan de la persona en los primeros meses?*
texte.Zwischen elf und halb zwölf verlassen ga: Between eleven and eleven-thirty, entire departments leave the building for coffee and a sandwich. It's not slacking off, but part of the workday – where things are discussed that don't come up in meetings.
texte.Viele arbeiten von neun bis vierzehn Uhr: Many work from nine to two, take a two-hour break, and then continue until six or seven. The *jornada intensiva* without a long break usually only happens in summer – and it's considered a privilege.
texte.*¿Me echas una mano?* ist die normale Fo: *¿Me echas una mano?* is the usual way to ask for help – not *¿Puedes ayudarme?*, which sounds more formal. If someone can't help, they'll say *Es que ando liado* ("I'm tied up right now"), rather than just saying no.
texte.*hablar + é = hablaré*. Die Endungen *-é: *hablar + é = hablaré*. The endings *-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án* are added to the full infinitive – the same for all three verb groups. It's the simplest tense in Spanish.
texte.*tener → tendré*, *poner → pondré*, *sal: *tener → tendré*, *poner → pondré*, *salir → saldré*, *venir → vendré*, *poder → podré*, *hacer → haré*, *decir → diré*, *querer → querré*, *saber → sabré*. The endings stay – only the stem changes.
texte.Für Pläne sagt man *voy a hablar*. Das F: For plans, you say *voy a hablar*. The future tense is mainly used for speculations about the PRESENT: *Serán las tres* (it's probably three), *Estará durmiendo* (he's probably sleeping). This surprises most learners.
texte.*Tengo pensado* und *tengo la intención: *Tengo pensado* and *tengo la intención de* are firm. *Me planteo* and *estoy pensando en* are considerations. *En principio* and *ya veremos* keep options open. This distinction is more important in professional settings than grammar.
texte.Es klingt freundlich und bedeutet oft: e: It sounds friendly but often means: probably not. To confirm, say *cuenta conmigo* or *te confirmo el jueves*. If you take *ya veremos* as a yes, you'll be waiting in vain.
texte.*A corto plazo* (Wochen bis Monate), *a: *A corto plazo* (weeks to months), *a medio plazo* (one to two years), *a largo plazo* (beyond that). These three categorize any plan – in conversations or job interviews.
texte.Noch nicht passiert? Dann Subjuntivo: Not happened yet? Then use Subjunctive
texte.*Cuando llegue* (wenn ich ankomme, noch: *Cuando llegue* (when I arrive, still uncertain) vs. *Cuando llego* (whenever I arrive, habit) vs. *Cuando llegué* (when I arrived, past). Only the future requires the Subjunctive.
texte.*cuando*, *en cuanto*, *hasta que*, *mie: *cuando*, *en cuanto*, *hasta que*, *mientras*, *siempre que*, *después de que* – all behave the same: Future with Subjunctive, habit and past with Indicative.
texte.antes de que ist die Ausnahme: antes de que is the exception
texte.Nach *antes de que* steht IMMER der Subj: After *antes de que*, ALWAYS use the Subjunctive, whether future, habit, or past: *Llámame antes de que salgas.* *Siempre me llamaba antes de que saliera.* Makes sense: What comes before hasn't happened yet.
texte.Dieselbe Person: *para* plus Infinitiv –: Same person: *para* plus infinitive – *Vengo para hablar contigo* (I come, I talk). Two people: *para que* plus Subjunctive – *Te lo doy para que lo leas* (I give, you read). Same rule as with emotion verbs.
texte.Förmlicher wird es mit a fin de que: More formal with a fin de que
texte.In E-Mails und Berichten liest man *a fi: In emails and reports, you see *a fin de que*, *con el fin de*, *con el objetivo de*. In conversation, it sounds stiff – just use *para que*. You need to understand both, but only use the simple form.
texte.no vaya a ser que – die Warnung: no vaya a ser que – the warning
texte.Wörtlich „nicht dass es sein möge, dass\: Literally "not that it may be that." It means: be careful, or something might happen. *Sal ya, no vaya a ser que pierdas el tren.* Always with Subjunctive, and very common in everyday speech.
texte.Es heißt *si tengo tiempo*, nie *si teng: It's *si tengo tiempo*, never *si tenga tiempo*. This rule has no exceptions. After *si*, use the indicative – present for possible situations, later the imperfect subjunctive for impossible ones.
texte.Präsens: *Si llueve, nos quedamos.* Futu: Present: *Si llueve, nos quedamos.* Future: *Si llueve, nos quedaremos.* Command: *Si llueve, quédate en casa.* All three are correct; in everyday speech, the present is most common.
texte.*Si puedo, voy* und *Voy si puedo* bedeu: *Si puedo, voy* and *Voy si puedo* mean the same. If the *si* part is first, use a comma; if it's last, don't. Nothing else changes – unlike in English, word order remains the same.
texte.Endungen an den Infinitiv, wie beim Futu: Endings added to the infinitive, like the future tense
texte.*hablar + ía = hablaría*. Die Endungen *: *hablar + ía = hablaría*. The endings *-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían* are added to the entire infinitive. The irregular stems are the same as in the future tense: *tendría*, *podría*, *haría*, *diría*.
texte.Höflichkeit: *¿Podrías ayudarme?* Rat: *: Politeness: *¿Podrías ayudarme?* Advice: *Yo que tú lo haría.* Speculation about the past: *Serían las ocho.* The same form, three very different uses – context clarifies it.
texte.Was das Futur für heute ist, ist er für: What the future tense is for now, it is for then
texte.*Serán las tres* – es wird wohl drei sei: *Serán las tres* – it’s probably three (now). *Serían las tres* – it was probably three (then). The speculation shifts with the tense. A neat pair to remember together.
texte.Nach *si* der Subjuntivo des Imperfekts,: After *si*, use the past subjunctive, followed by the conditional: *Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría.* Never the other way around. This structure is similar to English: "If I had time, I would travel."
texte.Die Form kommt aus dem Indefinido: The form comes from the simple past tense.
texte.Nimm die *ellos*-Form des Indefinido, st: Take the *ellos* form of the simple past, remove *-ron*, add *-ra*: *tuvieron → tuviera*, *pudieron → pudiera*, *fueron → fuera*, *supieron → supiera*. All irregularities carry over – nothing new to learn.
texte.Der eleganteste Rat im Spanischen. Statt: The most elegant advice in Spanish. Instead of saying *you should do this*, you say *Si yo fuera tú, lo haría así.* It sounds like a suggestion rather than a command – and is therefore more likely to be accepted.
texte.Der Konditional ist die Verhandlungsform: The conditional is the negotiation form.
texte.*Estaría dispuesto a…*, *Sería posible…*: *Estaría dispuesto a…*, *Sería posible…*, *Tendría que consultarlo…* The conditional makes any position sound negotiable. Demanding in the present tense – *quiero cuarenta mil* – closes the door before it was even open.
texte.Sie kommt fast immer, meist als *¿Cuál e: It almost always comes up, usually as *¿Cuál es su expectativa salarial?* If you don't want to name a number, say *Me gustaría conocer primero la banda salarial del puesto* – the salary range for the position. This is an accepted counter-question.
texte.Eine Forderung allein wirkt hart. *A cam: A demand alone can seem harsh. *A cambio de* turns it into a trade: *Aceptaría el sueldo a cambio de dos días de teletrabajo.* This way, the other side gets something that encourages agreement.
texte.Spanische Geschäftsmails kommen mit drei: Spanish business emails are concise, often just three paragraphs: introduction, main point, conclusion. Ending with *Un saludo* is enough – no double greetings or lengthy formalities. Length doesn't imply thoroughness, just complexity.
texte.Zu Kollegen: *Hola Ana,* … *Un saludo.*: To colleagues: *Hola Ana,* … *Un saludo.* To external contacts: *Buenos días:* … *Un cordial saludo.* To authorities: *Estimados señores:* … *Atentamente.* Using the middle form is almost always a safe choice.
texte.Wer eine Antwort anmahnt, beginnt mit *P: When you need to follow up for a response, start with *Perdona la insistencia* or *Disculpa que insista*. Then briefly state the matter, followed by *Cualquier duda, me dices.* Without this introduction, following up can seem demanding.
texte.Melden und Anliegen: *Buenos días, soy T: Introduce and state your purpose: *Buenos días, soy Tom de… Llamo por…* Clarify. Summarize: *Entonces quedamos en que…* Conclude: *Se lo confirmo por correo.* The third step is crucial – it prevents misunderstandings.
texte.Am Telefon buchstabiert man mit Städtena: On the phone, you spell using city names: *B de Barcelona*, *V de Valencia*, *H de Huelva*. This is especially important for *b* and *v*, which sound similar – hence the frequent question *¿be o uve?*
texte.Wo Deutsche eine Mail schreiben und drei: Where English speakers might send an email and wait for a few days, in Spain, people pick up the phone. A call is seen as efficient, not intrusive. The email follows – as confirmation, not as a substitute.
texte.*En primer lugar…*, *A continuación…*, *: *En primer lugar…*, *A continuación…*, *Por último…* These help your audience know where they are in the presentation. Without them, even good content can seem disorganized – with them, even a short presentation appears structured.
texte.*Ha aumentado*, *ha bajado*, *se mantien: *Has increased*, *has decreased*, *remains steady* – and then the size: *a fifteen percent*, *slightly*, *noticeably*. A number without direction and evaluation tells the audience nothing.
texte.Zwischenfragen gehören dazu: Questions in between are part of it
texte.In Spanien wird mitten im Vortrag gefrag: In Spain, people ask questions right in the middle of a presentation. If you deflect them, you seem unapproachable. Two responses work: *Good question, I'll explain now* or *If you don't mind, we'll cover that in two minutes.*
texte.Wer in Spanien Kritik vor der Gruppe äuß: In Spain, criticizing someone in front of the group never works – the other person needs to save face and will defend themselves, no matter how valid the point was. The phrase to use is *Do you have a moment?* and it effectively pauses the meeting.
texte.Von sich sprechen, nicht vom anderen: Speak about yourself, not the other person
texte.*Me he sentido al margen* statt *Me has: *I felt left out* instead of *You left me out.* The first sentence describes a feeling that no one can dispute. The second is an accusation – and triggers the *defensive* response that ends the conversation.
texte.Ein Konfliktgespräch ohne Ergebnis kommt: A conflict discussion without a resolution will resurface in two weeks. *Looking ahead, can we agree that you'll let me know beforehand?* Then briefly say *no hard feelings* – this resolves the issue and keeps the relationship intact.
texte.Deutsche loben zurückhaltend und kritisi: English speakers often praise modestly and criticize openly – in Spain, it's the opposite. *Congratulations* is said in front of everyone, often enthusiastically. The suggestion for improvement comes later, in private, and starts with what was done well.
texte.*Yo cambiaría el final* ist ein Vorschla: *I would change the ending* is a suggestion. *Change the ending* is a command. And *I'd give it another thought* is the friendliest way to say: It's not quite there yet.
texte.*¿Cómo lo ves?* macht aus einem Urteil e: *¿Cómo lo ves?* turns a judgment into a conversation. If you want feedback yourself, ask *¿Qué le cambiarías?* – more specific than *¿Qué te parece?*, which usually just gets a *muy bien*.
texte.*Ojalá pueda* heißt: Es ist möglich, ich: *Ojalá pueda* means: It's possible, I hope so. *Ojalá pudiera* means: I can't, and I know it. It's the same distinction as with the unreal *if* – only here, the wish stands alone, without a condition.
texte.Der falsche Freund des Kapitels. *Me hac: The false friend of the chapter. *Me hace ilusión* doesn't mean "I'm deluding myself," but "I'm looking forward to it" – the warm anticipation of something nice. A very Spanish word without a precise English equivalent.
texte.Wo Deutsche einen Plan erwarten, sagen S: Where English speakers might expect a plan, Spaniards often say *ya veremos*. It's not an evasion, but an attitude: You don't commit to what you don't know. If you hear it, don't press further – the answer is the answer.

texte.Präsens, beide Vergangenheiten und ihr U: Present, both past tenses and their difference, future, conditional, the subjunctive in present and past, real and unreal conditions. This is the complete framework of the language. What remains now is not a system anymore – just vocabulary.
texte.*Aunque me equivoque* – auch wenn ich Fe: *Aunque me equivoque* – even if I make mistakes. If you wait until your sentences are perfect, you'll never speak. If you talk and get corrected, you'll be fluent in half a year. This sequence can't be reversed.
texte.Ohne Kurs zerfällt eine Sprache in etwa: Without practice, a language fades in about a year. With twenty minutes a day, it stays: a series without subtitles, a podcast while cooking, a conversation a week. *El idioma se mantiene usándolo* – no more method is needed from here.
